premise: Two notes sit in one folder. Find which one holds the book title and which one points the way.

rescue: If a date turns up, ask the helper to quote it. Reopen the two files and compare.

premise: Change a spelling mistake on one line of a list. The other lines need to stay in place.
before: Create catalog.txt with these three lines in order: Dock Notes, Dock Notse, Dock Notes Archive. Use a separate line for each. Stop so I can check the file.

rescue: If one line disappears, ask for the original order and both copies. Check the whole list again.

premise: Make a tiny page with a question on one side and a hidden answer you can reveal.

rescue: If the words change on the button but the answer stays put, ask the helper to change both on each click.

premise: One row has zero minutes. Another has no time at all. Find out why only one belongs in the count.
before: Make input.csv with the heading ID,minutes and rows A,15 then B,0 then C, then D,oops. Write summarize.py in Python 3. Count rows with numbers, including zero. Add their minutes. List the IDs of skipped rows. Use the tools built into Python and run the file.

rescue: If only A counts at first, ask the helper to check for an empty cell before turning the text into a number.

premise: A computer can put 10 ahead of 2 when it sorts words. Teach a scoreboard to sort numbers instead.
before: Create sort.html with a Sort button. Start with the three text values 10, 2 and 0. On click, show what JavaScript sort() returns with no extra rule. Leave this first version as it is until I test it.

rescue: If the second 2 vanishes, ask for a sorted list that keeps every entry. Count the four items.

premise: Teach one reader where two versions of a game save their points.
before: Plan a Python reader for these three records: {"version":1,"points":7}, {"version":2,"score":0}, {"version":3,"score":99}. The first version uses points. The second uses score. Raise ValueError for an unknown version. Show the planned tests before writing files.
try: Read the plan. Ask for reader.py and test_reader.py. Ask the helper to run python3 -m unittest -v. Find a passing test for each known version. Add one test for version 2 with no score field. Keep the test for version 3 and run the checks again.

premise: Build a clock rule for a desk that opens at ten at night and closes at two in the morning.
before: Plan is_open(hour, minute) in Python. The desk opens at 22:00 and closes at 02:00. Count the opening minute. Treat the closing minute as closed. Times use a 24-hour clock. Raise ValueError for a bad hour or minute. Show a test table first.

why: Think of an overnight shift as two pieces on a clock: late tonight and early tomorrow.
rescue: If midnight shows closed, check both pieces of the shift. Check the minute just before and exactly at closing.

premise: A report can have an empty page with an arrow to more rows. Follow the arrows and catch a loop.
before: Build a Python test with pretend pages. Start at p1. Its value list is ["A"] and its @odata.nextLink is p2. Page p2 has [] and links to p3. Page p3 has ["C"] and no link. Record every page you ask for. Stop with an error if a link repeats. Keep the test on this computer.

after: It visits p1, p2 and p3 in order. The result is A, C. The reader reports a loop before asking for p2 a second time.
why: Turning a blank page is easy when the book gives you a next-page arrow. A bookmark helps you spot a page you saw already.
rescue: If C is gone, ask the helper to stop when there is no next link. An empty list alone is not the end.

premise: Let someone read the rules and return to the game using only keys.
before: Build dialog.html. Add a Rules button. Enter opens a box with a heading, the words Two players take turns, and a Close button. Move the keyboard highlight to Close. Keep it inside the box until Escape or Close shuts it. Return the highlight to Rules.
try: Open the page. Press Tab until Rules is highlighted. Press Enter. Use Tab and Shift with Tab to see where the highlight goes. Press Escape. Check the highlight. Open Rules again. This time activate Close with the keyboard.
after: The box opens. You can read its rule. The keyboard highlight reaches Close and stays in the open box. Both ways put the highlight back on Rules. While the box is closed, you cannot tab to its Close button.
why: The highlight is your place on the page. It should return to where you paused the game.
rescue: If the highlight disappears, ask the helper to remember the opening button and focus it when the box closes.

premise: Save two tiny book files in the browser. Make sure the newer edition takes the place of the old one.
before: Build a little book on localhost with index.html, chapter.txt saying edition A, and sw.js. This last file is a browser helper. Have it save the page and chapter for offline use. Show Ready offline once it can serve this page. Remove only this book’s old saved copies when a new edition takes over. Give me a command to serve the folder.
try: Run the given command. Open its local address. Wait for Ready offline. Take the browser offline and reload this same page. Go online. Ask the helper to change the chapter to edition B and the name of its saved copy. Close old book tabs, reopen online and wait. Go offline again and reload.
after: Edition A still opens. The page can read its chapter without a network connection. The reader now shows B offline. In the browser storage view the old copy of this book is gone.
why: Imagine replacing a packed lunch before you leave. A new label alone does not change what is in the bag.
rescue: If A returns, close all old book tabs. Open online, wait for the new helper to take over, then test offline again.

premise: Two slips may have the same number of points. Use the slip ID to tell a real second score from a repeat.
before: Use Python and a temporary SQLite database. Store each score ID just once. Enter A,+40 and B,+40. Send A,+40 again. Reject a repeat ID with a changed amount. Also send C,+10 from two separate connections at the same time. Have the database enforce the one-ID rule.
try: Ask to see the stored rows after the repeat and again after both copies of C arrive. Run the tests on a fresh database. Repeat the two-connection test on fresh data. Then try A,+41 against the finished database.
after: The repeat leaves A and B, total 80. After C there are three rows and the total is 90. The tool flags the change. A still has 40 points and the total stays 90.
why: A printed ticket number belongs to one sale. Receiving another copy does not mean someone bought another ticket.
rescue: If the total reaches 100, ask for a rule in the database that blocks a second row with the same ID. Test both connections again.

premise: Stack three sets of settings. The top set can turn an option off or choose zero as a limit.
before: In Python, start with reminders=true and limit=10. The site sets limit=5. The user sets reminders=false and limit=0. Use the last set that actually names a setting. Show its value and where it came from. Reject a named value of null and unknown setting names. Keep the input lists unchanged.
try: Run the first example. Remove limit from the user settings and run again. Then remove the site limit too. Try reminders=false with a misspelled setting called typo_lim. In another test, set limit to null. Look at the original lists after each run.
after: At first the user gives false and 0. Removing the user limit gives 5 from the site. Removing both gives 10 from the defaults. Both bad inputs raise an error. The original settings still match what you put in.
why: Zero and off are real choices. A blank value and a missing setting each need their own rule.
rescue: If 0 becomes 5, ask whether the key is present, instead of asking whether its value is positive.

premise: Find a way to save points that both an old game and a new game can read.
before: In Python make an old reader that looks for points. Make a new reader that accepts points or score and rejects different values when both appear. Build an old writer that saves only points. Build a second writer that saves both fields with the same value. Test both readers with both writers for 0 and -7.
try: Draw two reader columns and two writer rows. Mark each box after the helper runs its tests. Add a writer that saves only score. Try both readers. Then give them a record with points=3 and score=4. Ask which readers should be updated first.
after: All four pairs read both 0 and -7 correctly. The score-only file works with the new reader. The old reader gets 3 from the mixed file. The new reader rejects that file.
why: Keep writing both labels while older readers still need the first one. Let all readers learn the new label before retiring the old one.
rescue: If both readers pass everything, inspect the test that uses only score. The old reader must notice its missing points field.

premise: Two teams report the same outage. Combine their time blocks without counting the overlap twice.
before: Use Python and UTC times on January 1–2, 2027. A runs from Jan 1 23:50 to Jan 2 00:10. On Jan 2, B runs 00:05–00:20, C runs 00:20–00:25, and D runs 00:08–00:09. Count each minute of downtime once. End times mark when service is back. Accept an interval of zero minutes. Reject an end earlier than its start.
try: Draw the four lines on a time strip. Ask the helper for the total. Shuffle the input, repeat A, and try D with the same start and end. Add Jan 2 01:00 to 01:02. Then feed the tool one interval with the end earlier than its start.
after: The combined stretch is 35 minutes. Shuffle, repeats and an empty stretch add zero minutes. The separated two minutes raise the total to 37. The reversed interval gets a clear error.
why: A minute when two notices say service is down is still one minute on your clock.
rescue: If the total is too large, merge overlapping blocks before adding their lengths. Check that C starts just when B ends.

premise: Pretend the power goes out while scores are being saved. Make the next run pick up at the right place.
before: Build a local Python importer with temporary SQLite. Input is R1,+8 then R2,-3 then R3,+5. Save each row and its place marker together so both are kept or neither is. Add a practice switch to stop just after saving row two. Resume, then run the whole file again. Reject repeats with a changed amount.
try: Stop after row two. Open a new process and start the importer again. Compare its rows with one clean run through the file. Read the whole file again. Then send a new file beginning with R2,-9 to the database that already holds all three rows.
after: After the stop there are two rows, total 5, marker 2. After resuming there are three rows, total 10, marker 3. The full repeat adds nothing. The changed R2 raises an error and its stored amount remains -3.
why: A row and its bookmark belong together. Saving just one can cause a missing row or a double score after a restart.
rescue: If the last row is lost, check when the bookmark is saved. If a duplicate changes the total, compare both the ID and its stored value.

premise: A note names a pier and a day. Find the two facts it gives and spot the one it leaves out.
before: Read just this note: Harbor shuttle boards at Pier 4 on March 8. Bring the blue ticket. Return three lines called Pier, Date and Time. Write unknown if the note leaves a fact out. Use the date exactly as given.
try: Find each answer in the note with your finger. Read the date carefully. In a new chat, add Boarding begins at 09:15 to the note. Keep the same question and run again.
after: The three answers are Pier 4, March 8 and unknown. No year appears. Only Time changes. It now says 09:15. The date still has no year.
why: Leaving a box empty can be more helpful than making up an answer that sounds right.
rescue: If a time or year appears in the first answer, ask the helper to show the exact words that prove it.

premise: Write one standing rule for a stack of topic cards. Each answer should use only its own card.
before: Return only Topic | Owner. Copy the stated topic and owner exactly. Use UNASSIGNED when the card has no named owner.
try: Read the first reply. In the same chat send Card K4. Topic: Trains. Owner: Team One. Keep each answer on its own row. Send Card R9. Topic: Maps. Look at its owner box before reading earlier rows.
after: The first row is Ferries | UNASSIGNED. The second is Trains | Team One. The last row is Maps | UNASSIGNED. Team One belongs only to Trains.
why: Imagine giving three envelopes separate address labels. The name on one label should never slide onto its neighbor.
rescue: If Maps gets Team One, add that each card starts with empty fields. Run all three cards again in order.

premise: Teach the helper when to choose one tray, two trays or the tray marked unknown.
before: Use MAIL for a bounced letter and FILES for a document that will not open. Use BOTH when both things happen. Use UNKNOWN for just please help. Label four slips in order: A mail came back, B document does not load, C please help, D mail returned and document fails. Give just the ID and tray for each.
try: Cover the reply with your hand. Predict the four trays yourself, then compare them one by one. Replace slip A with the cafeteria is closed. Start a fresh chat with the same examples. Try the whole set again.
after: A is MAIL, B is FILES, C is UNKNOWN and D is BOTH. Only A changes. It now goes in UNKNOWN.
why: A label says what is in a slip. A slip with too few clues belongs in the unknown tray until someone adds detail.
rescue: If D gets just one tray, add a new teaching example with two problems and the label BOTH. Test with the original slips again.

premise: A draft and an approved notice give different days. Find the date a reader can actually use.
before: Read just these three slips. M1 says Draft: Pier 2 opens June 3. M2 says Approved: Pier 2 opens June 8. M3 says Approved: Pier 4 opens June 9. When is Pier 2 approved to open? When does it close? Give the slip ID and its words for each answer, or say no source gives it.
try: Look at the pier number and the word Approved on each slip. Match both clues before accepting a date. Remove M2 and ask again in a fresh chat. Check whether an approved date for Pier 2 still exists.
after: M2 supports June 8. None of the slips gives a closing date. The approved opening date for Pier 2 is now unknown.
why: The right day on the wrong pier's sign is still the wrong answer.
rescue: If June 9 appears, ask the helper to quote its pier number. If June 3 appears, ask whether its slip was approved.

premise: Turn three launch cards into records an app can read. Leave a missing date empty on purpose.
before: {"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"id":{"type":"string"},"date":{"type":["string","null"]}},"required":["id","date"]}}
try: Compare each record with its card. Look closely at the middle date field. It should hold the empty marker, without quotes. Use the same shape in a fresh run. Change only C3 to 2027-05-10. Compare all three records.
after: The dates are 2027-04-02, null and 2027-05-09, in order. Only C3 changes to May 10. C2 stays empty.
why: A form with two labeled boxes is easier for a program to read than a different sentence for every card.
rescue: If C2 contains a made-up date, ask for an empty date when the card gives none. Check the field in the actual result.

premise: Read the math the helper ran. Check a zero round, a missing round and a negative score.
before: Use code execution to total this sample table. Heading: player,points. Rows: Red,12 then Blue,-3 then Red,0 then Blue,8 then Red,blank. Skip the word blank. Count a real 0 as a played round. Show points and played rounds per team and points for everyone together.
try: Open the code and its printed result. Add each team's points on paper before comparing. Replace Blue,8 with Blue,-8 and run again. Count the played rounds a second time.
after: Red has 12 in two rounds. Blue has 5 in two rounds. The grand total is 17. Blue now has -11. The grand total is 1. Each team still has two played rounds.
why: A zero-point turn still happened. A blank tells you that the turn has no score written down.
rescue: If Red has one round, mark a zero as played. If Red has three, make sure the word blank is skipped.

premise: Give two helpers the same parking puzzle. Score the math before picking a favorite answer.
before: A pretend lot charges 2 dollars per started hour up to 8 dollars. Entries at or after 18:00 cost 3 dollars flat. All visits end the same day. A stays 17:30–19:45, B stays 18:00–18:20 and C stays 09:00–15:00. Give each fee and say which clock time picks the rule.
try: Run it in two fresh chats with different models or thinking levels. Give one point per correct fee and one for using the entry time. Record scores out of four. Move A's entry to 18:01. Keep the same exit. Try the change with both models and record how long each takes.
after: A costs 6 dollars, B costs 3 and C costs 8. Entry time picks the rule. A now costs 3 dollars. The other fees stay the same. A tie is a possible result.
why: An answer can look neat and still use the wrong clock. An answer key gives both helpers the same test.
rescue: If a helper charges A the evening price in the first round, ask which time on the ticket it used.

premise: A question is sent to a pretend book catalog. Watch the request go out and the shelf number come back.
before: {"name":"lookup_book","description":"Look up an exact book ID","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"id":{"type":"string"}},"required":["id"]}}
try: Look for a call to lookup_book with id BK17. Use the tool reply box, if offered, to return {"found":true,"shelf":"H-04"}. Then read the answer. In a fresh run ask for BK99. Return {"found":false} to that lookup. Check what the helper says.
after: First comes a request for BK17. Only after the tool reply does the answer give H-04. The shelf is unknown. No invented shelf number appears.
why: The model is like a librarian asking someone to check the shelf. Asking for a lookup does not supply the answer.
rescue: If your screen cannot enter a tool reply, write the request and reply as two lines on paper. A practice dialogue is not proof a real tool ran.

premise: Use a picture with two colored labels. Run the same question again without the picture.
before: QZ
try: Compare its answer with the local picture. Check position as well as color and letter. Open a fresh chat. Use the same words, this time without the screenshot. Run the question again.
after: The left panel is blue Q. The right panel is red Z. The reply asks for an image or says it cannot see the panels.
why: A helper can remember an earlier answer. Starting a fresh chat helps test what the picture itself contributed.
rescue: If colored labels appear without the picture, check the new chat for attachments and earlier messages.

premise: Build a small real form. Let a reader fix dates and export the two cards once both are ready.
before: Build a page with two editable cards. N1 is Harbor dated 2027-06-03. N2 is Rail with an empty date. Mark missing dates Needs review. Add Export JSON. It may export only real calendar dates in year-month-day order. Show the finished records in the preview. Use local sample data.
try: Leave N2 blank. Try to export. Next try February 30, 2027. Watch the button or the error message. Set N2 to 2027-06-04. Export and count the records. Clear N1 and try to export again.
after: Neither a blank nor February 30 can be exported. Both full cards export once. Clearing N1 blocks the next export.
why: A string with three numbers can still describe a day that never happens. Test the real calendar as well as the spelling.
rescue: If February 30 turns into a March date, ask for the date the user typed to be compared with the date the code checked.

premise: A rule can be approved today and start later. Work out which rule was in force on each day.
before: Consider only approved records effective on or before the query date. Use the latest effective date. If two eligible records tie on that date and disagree, return CONFLICT with both IDs. With no eligible record, return UNKNOWN.
try: Check approval first. Cross off any rule that starts after the day in the question. Pick the latest one still on the list. Add P4, approved for July 12 with cap 5. Run the same three days again using the rule in the box above.
after: The answers are UNKNOWN, 4 from P1, and 6 from P3. July 12 is CONFLICT with P3 and P4. Neither earlier answer changes.
why: If two approved signs for the same day disagree, finding the disagreement is the useful answer.
rescue: If 9 appears, check P2's draft label. If one July 12 rule wins after P4 arrives, check for a tie on the start date.

premise: Find a boat's ID, then use that ID to look up its next stop. Try both a match and a missing boat.
before: [{"name":"find_vessel","description":"Resolve a nickname","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"nickname":{"type":"string"}},"required":["nickname"]}},{"name":"get_route","description":"Fetch a route by exact vessel ID","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"vessel_id":{"type":"string"}},"required":["vessel_id"]}}]
try: When the first tool asks about Wren, reply {"found":true,"id":"V42"}. Check the next call uses V42. Reply {"next_stop":"Cove"}. Try Sparrow in a fresh chat. Answer the first lookup with {"found":false}. Watch for any more requests.
after: The requests are find_vessel for Wren and get_route for V42. The final answer is Cove. There is no second lookup for Sparrow. Its next stop is unknown.
why: Think of a locker number on a claim slip. You need the number from the first desk before asking the second desk to open anything.
rescue: If your screen cannot send tool replies, act out each call on paper. If a route is guessed, ask where the boat ID came from.

premise: Try two ways to explain a color rule. Check whether the better explanation also works on numbers it has never seen.
before: Use RED for a whole number of 10 or more, AMBER for 5 to 9 and GREEN for 0 to 4. Use UNKNOWN for missing, negative or non-whole numbers. Give just ID and label. Try A=0, B=4, C=5, D=9, E=10, F=missing, G=-1, H=4.5.
try: Score one point per right label. In a new chat with the same model add this rule: First check that the number exists and is whole and at least zero. Score it again. Try both wordings in fresh chats on I=7, J=11, K=2, L=1.25. Record each score even if they tie.
after: A through H should give GREEN, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER, RED, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN. The new answer key is AMBER, RED, GREEN, UNKNOWN. A good score on the first eight alone cannot settle the comparison.
why: Like spelling practice, a new word list shows whether you learned the rule or memorized the earlier answers.
rescue: If 4.5 becomes GREEN, ask for a whole-number check before the color rule. Keep the four new cases out of the teaching examples.

premise: Count what the practice helpers cost, including tries you pay for twice. All prices here are made up for a math game.
before: Turn on code execution. For A through H, Quick costs 2 cents per case and gets A–E right. Deep costs 8 cents per case and gets A–G right. Test Quick alone, Deep alone, and Quick on all followed by Deep on E,F,G,H. On those four keep Deep's answer. Report total cents, correct answers and cents per correct answer.
try: Write eight letters on paper. Mark each paid try and circle each final correct answer. Compare your totals with the printed math. Take G off the list of second tries. Run the math again. Check which answer is now lost.
after: Quick costs 16 cents for 5 right, or 3.2 each. Deep costs 64 for 7, or about 9.14 each. Both stages cost 48 for 7, or about 6.86 each. The cost is 40 cents for 6 right, or about 6.67 each. G now has Quick's wrong answer.
why: Cost per win is the money spent divided by the number of good answers. A cheaper win can still leave more questions wrong.
rescue: If the second route costs only 32 cents, add the 16 cents spent on the first eight tries.

premise: Build a page that lets you approve a draft only when the date, bay and quoted words all match the source.
before: In Build, make a private practice app. L1 reads Bay 7 opens 2027-08-04. L2 reads Bay 9 opening date pending. Ask Gemini to suggest a bay, date or null, line ID and exact quote for each. Show the source beside the row. In ordinary code, check bay, date and quote before allowing approval. Add Run fixture checks to test saved examples without an AI call.
try: Try four checks: the true Bay 7 row, Bay 9 with no date, Bay 9 claiming L1's date, and Bay 7 quoting words that never appear. Press the test button. Approve a valid row. Change its date. Check the row and approval again. Also try to approve a row that fails.
after: The two true rows pass. The crossed bay and invented quote fail. A changed row needs a fresh review. A row that fails its checks cannot be approved.
why: A real date copied from the wrong line is still a wrong answer. The source and the answer must refer to the same thing.
rescue: If the crossed row passes, add a check that the bay in the quote matches the bay on the card. Run all four saved checks again.

premise: A mail notice tells you when search will be fixed. Who owns the work?
before: Notice A. Mail search maintenance, Saturday 09:00–09:30 UTC. Message delivery will continue.
try: Put your finger on the start and end times in the notice. Read the sentence about delivery. Search the same notice for any owner before accepting that cell. Add “Owner: Support Desk” and call it Notice B. Ask for a fresh table.
after: Notice A gives a 30-minute window, 09:00 to 09:30 UTC. Its owner is unspecified. B names Support Desk. Both notices say delivery will continue.
why: A part of a service can be under repair while another part still works.
rescue: If the table says all mail stops, point to “Message delivery will continue” and ask for a correction.

premise: Three messages mention two days. One is booked and one is only an idea.
before:
M1 Approver: Tuesday is booked.
M2 Organizer: Could we use Wednesday instead?
M3 Approver: I will check.
try: Mark booked with a check and could with a question mark. Ask whether the last message resolves the question or simply promises a reply. Add “M4 Approver: Wednesday is now booked. Cancel Tuesday.” Ask for the list again.
after: Tuesday is booked in M1. Wednesday is a request in M2. The approver still owes an answer after M3. Wednesday is now booked. Tuesday is canceled. M4 is the key message.
why: Someone saying they will check a date has not yet said yes to it.
rescue: If Wednesday appears as booked too soon, ask what word in M3 confirms it. Then read M1 again.

premise: Users need to know what to do. The help desk needs the same facts in a form it can scan.
before: Build 12. A display bug affects iPad only. Fix rolls out Tuesday 14:00 UTC. Restart the app after rollout. Windows needs no action.
try: Underline the device, time and action in the release note. Find each of those facts in the user notice and again in the desk bullets. Replace the rollout time with “Rollout time pending.” Make both notes again.
after: Both versions say iPad, Tuesday at 14:00 UTC and restart after the update. Windows needs no action. Both now say the time is pending. Neither gives a new time.
why: Different readers can need different words without changing any facts.
rescue: If the draft gives an Android step, point to the two devices the note names. Ask it to drop extra guesses.

premise: A chat starts before the meeting record. Find the decision that someone actually made.
before:
09:03 chat C1 Recorder: Could exports run nightly?
09:10 transcript begins
09:12 T1 Approver: I approve weekly exports.
09:13 T2 Recorder: I will own the export job.
try: Put T1 beside the decision and T2 beside the owner. Cover T1 with paper. Ask which claim has now lost its support. Remove T1. Start a fresh chat with just the remaining lines and repeat the request.
after: Weekly exports were approved in T1. The Recorder takes the job in T2. No due date appears. The owner is still visible. There is no longer proof of an approved schedule.
why: A missing line can change what you can say. Someone asking for nightly exports is not giving approval.
rescue: If the answer calls nightly a decision, ask which line says yes to it.

premise: One sample account has two plans. A row can also be a repeat.
before:
Row,Person,Plan
1,u1,A
2,u1,B
3,u2,A
4,u2,A
try: Write out u1+A, u1+B and u2+A. Mark the second u2+A as already seen. Compare that list with the four raw rows. Add a fifth row with an empty person field and plan B. Ask for the same counts and a list of rows to check.
after: Four rows give three pairs and two people, u1 and u2. Five rows remain. One needs a person. The known totals stay at three pairs and two people.
why: Counting tickets and counting guests are different jobs. One guest can hold two tickets.
rescue: If u2 appears twice in the people count, cross its second appearance off a paper list.

premise: A poll went to twelve sites. Nine replied and six said yes. Which share can you claim?
before: Pilot A. Invited: 12 sites. Responded: 9. Respondents supporting extension: 6.
try: Draw twelve dots. Circle the nine replies and color six of those dots. Compare six of the circled dots with six of all twelve. Ask whether “Two thirds of all pilot sites said yes” fits the data. Give the slide a better title.
after: Six of nine who replied said yes. Six of twelve invited sites are known to support the idea. A correct title can say “Six of nine replies support the plan.” The other three replies are missing.
why: The bottom number of a fraction tells you which group your sentence is about.
rescue: If a missing reply counts as no, label it unknown instead. Keep the count of actual replies at nine.

premise: Build a rule for a mail queue and try the values right at its edges.
before:
ID,Minutes
A,14
B,15
C,29
D,30
E,
F,-1
try: Draw four boxes for the four labels. Place 14 and 15 using the exact edge rule. Put the blank in its own box before doing any math. Change A from 14 to 15 and recalculate.
after: A is normal, B and C are watch, D is investigate, E and F are invalid. Normal drops to 0 and watch rises to 3. Investigate stays 1 and invalid stays 2.
why: The time 15 belongs in exactly one box. A missing reading stays missing.
rescue: If the empty row becomes normal, put the blank check ahead of the number checks.

premise: A new rule starts on a certain date. Check the date before checking group size.
before:
V1 effective Jan 1: groups up to 20 may move.
V2 effective Feb 1: groups up to 30 may move unless flagged; flagged groups are held.
A Jan 31 size 25; B Feb 1 size 30 clear; C Feb 2 size 12 flagged; D Feb 3 size 12 flag unknown.
try: Make a tiny calendar with January 31, February 1 and February 2. Write the rule edition over each day and then read its flag rule. Move the V2 start to February 2. Ask again about B and C.
after: A is held, B allowed, C held and D unknown. B now uses V1 and is held. C still uses V2 and is held because of its flag.
why: Rules work like a dated bus pass. You need the version valid on the day of the trip.
rescue: If B stays allowed, compare its February 1 date with the new February 2 start.

premise: Two archive rules fit on a card. Ask a helper to stay within them.
before:
P1 Standard archive request: 5 business days.
P2 Urgent archive request: 1 business day.
Q1 Standard archive time? Q2 Restore time? Q3 Archive time?
try: Look up Q1 in P1. Search P1 and P2 for restore before answering Q2. For Q3, ask which archive rule you should use. Change the urgent rule to 2 business days. Ask how long an urgent request now takes.
after: Q1 takes 5 business days under P1. Q2 is not covered. Q3 needs the request type. The answer is 2 business days and cites P2.
why: Looking up a rule is different from inventing one that sounds fair.
rescue: If the helper gives a restore time, ask which of the two clauses mentions restore.

premise: A big batch and a small one had different results. Work out the rate for all items together.
before:
Batch,Attempted,Completed
West,80,72
East,20,10
Idle,0,0
try: Add the finished items first, then the attempted items. Divide once. For the other result, write each batch percentage and average those two values. Change the small batch to 22 completed out of 20. Ask whether a new final rate is valid.
after: 72/80 is 90%. 10/20 is 50%. Together 82/100 is 82%. The simple average of 90% and 50% is 70%. The 22/20 row must be fixed. Hold the new rate until the count makes sense.
why: One batch has four times as many items. Giving the two percentages equal weight answers a different question.
rescue: If the total says 70%, ask for the total number finished and total number attempted before dividing.

premise: A lookup list puts one mailbox in two departments. Catch the extra copy before you report usage.
before:
Usage: m1=10, m2=20.
Map: m1→North, m1→South, m2→East.
try: Write m1 on two output slips and m2 on one to see how a blind lookup gives 40. Then return to the two original usage rows to find 30. Remove the m1 to South link and repeat the checks.
after: The source has 30 GB. Copying every match gives 40 GB. The disputed 10 GB belongs to m1. All 30 GB now have one clear department. The result matches the source total.
why: Sticking two labels on the same box does not double what is inside.
rescue: If the total reaches 40, list every copy of m1 with its 10 GB beside it.

premise: A delay starts before midnight on one clock. Compare times after putting them all in UTC.
before:
A Jan 5 23:55 -0600: delay observed.
B Jan 6 06:02 +0000: queue peaked.
C Jan 6 01:10 -0500: recovery observed.
D 00:59 offset/date unknown: configuration note.
try: Move A forward six hours and C forward five hours. Put both converted times on January 6 before counting the minutes. Add January 6 and -0500 to D. Ask for the ordered timeline once more.
after: A is 05:55 UTC on January 6. C is 06:10 UTC. The gap is 15 minutes. D has no date or offset. D now fits at 05:59 UTC. Its position alone cannot prove it caused the delay.
why: Two clocks may show different hours at the same moment. Convert them before comparing them.
rescue: If A falls a day early, add the six hours and carry the date past midnight.

premise: A backup expires after an hour. One test is still waiting. Try the rule on both sides of the time limit.
before:
Rule: approved rollback; successful backup within 60 min; all smoke tests pass.
R1 rollback approved. B1 backup successful 09:00 UTC. T1 two passed, one pending.
Times: 10:00 and 10:01 UTC, same day.
try: Make three check boxes for approval, backup and tests. At each clock time, fill each box independently before deciding the result. Change T1 to three passed and ask for each verdict again.
after: At 10:00 the backup is still good but a test is pending. At 10:01 the backup is also too old. Both verdicts are HOLD. 10:00 becomes GO. At 10:01 it is still HOLD.
why: A fresh backup cannot make a missing test pass. Each check must stand on its own.
rescue: If both times say GO, subtract the backup time from each clock time before checking the hour limit.

premise: A request can arrive twice when a button is tapped again. Keep one copy of the same job.
before:
R1 | project alpha
R1 | project alpha
R2 | project beta
R1 | project gamma
try: Keep a little ledger with ID and text. Before each event, find its ID in the ledger and decide whether the row is new, equal or different. Add R3 with project alpha. Count the rows again.
after: The four requests give create, reuse, create, conflict. R1 still holds project alpha. R3 creates its own row. There are now three rows, one for each different ID.
why: Matching text does not mean matching requests. The receipt number tells you which request is which.
rescue: If the second R1 made a new row, look up its ID before adding anything.

premise: The report must reach 95% and someone must actually approve. A wish or a promise is not a yes.
before:
G1 gate: >=95% complete AND owner approval.
R1 North 48/50. R2 South 47/50.
M1 owner: I can review tomorrow.
M2 participant: We should move ahead.
try: First add 48 and 47. Next read the owner’s exact words. Put the number check and the approval check on separate lines in all three outputs. Add M3 with explicit owner approval. Then change R2 to 46/50 and ask again.
after: 48 plus 47 gives 95 of 100. M1 promises a review. M2 is a suggestion. The verdict is HOLD. M3 makes the original result GO. With 94 of 100 done the decision returns to HOLD.
why: Two locks need two keys. A good score opens one lock and approval opens the other.
rescue: If a slide says ready with 94 complete, recompute its count and match the slide title with the check table.

premise: A small program sorts mail by size. Predict what happens to a message right on the dividing line.
try: Find the line with >=. Say it as greater than or equal to. Compare the answers for 24 and 25. Change only >= to > in the file. Save it and ask Claude to read the same four sizes again.
after: The four answers are normal, normal, large and large. Now 25 is normal. Each other answer stays the same.
why: A line that says 25 and up includes the person standing on 25. A line that says over 25 starts one step later.
rescue: If the answers all stay the same, check the saved file. Ask Claude to quote the sign it sees now.

premise: Read a tiny file of teams. Tell the next reader which rows still need someone to look after them.
before:
name,owner
Shipping,Team A
Facilities,
Design Lab,Team B
Front Desk,
try: Count the rows on paper. Cross off each row that already has a team listed in its owner box. Put Lead C in the Facilities owner box. Save the table and ask Claude to build the note again.
after: There are four rows. Two have owners. Facilities and Front Desk are unknown. Three rows now have an owner. Only Front Desk is unknown.
why: A blank owner is a useful thing to show the next reader. Skipping the row would hide the work left to do.
rescue: If all four are called owned, check the owner column. The first column names the item, even when its owner is blank.

premise: Give a project its own short rule card. See whether a new chat in the same folder follows it.
before:
For every release note, use exactly these two Markdown headings in order:
## Change
## Verification
Use one plain sentence under each heading.
try: Read the two headings in release.md. Confirm that each has one sentence using just the supplied facts. Start a fresh Claude Code session in the same folder. Ask for release-next.md about a fixed date label tested on one device. Leave the heading rule out of this second request.
after: The headings are Change and Verification, in that order. The check mentions two devices. The second note has the same two headings. It says one device and describes the date label.
why: A rule kept with the project is like a recipe card kept inside the box. It is there the next time you open it.
rescue: If the second note repeats the reminder fix, ask Claude to use only today's two facts. Check it reopened the same folder.

premise: Strip extra spaces and keep one copy of each address in its original order.
before:
input separated by |	expected separated by |
 A@Example.test |a@example.test|B@EXAMPLE.TEST	a@example.test|b@example.test
 | Z@example.test | 	z@example.test
try: Compare the input and expected columns in the file. Ask Claude to point out the repeated address in the first row. Try the list [" Z@X ","a@x","z@x"," "]. Then try an empty list. Print the two results.
after: The first row keeps a@example.test then b@example.test. The blank pieces in the second row drop out. The results are ["z@x","a@x"] and [].
why: A list of seats can keep the first ticket number it sees. A repeated ticket does not need another seat.
rescue: If a@x moves to the front, ask the code to keep the first-seen order and remove the extra sort.

premise: Decide what the rule should do before writing a single line of the program.
before:
Mailbox quota warning begins at 90 percent inclusive.
Below 90 is OK.
A missing percentage must be UNKNOWN.
try: Read the proposed answers for 89, 90 and None. Here None means the source supplied no percentage. Allow edits to the practice folder. Ask Claude to write classify(value) in quota.py and run those three tests.
after: The plan says 89 is OK, 90 is WARNING and a missing value is UNKNOWN. It comes before file edits. The finished program gives OK, WARNING and UNKNOWN in order.
why: Choose the answers before seeing the code. Then a test can catch a wrong guess in the code.
rescue: If None shows OK, ask the code to check for a missing value before comparing numbers.

premise: A short report hides a group when its owner is missing. Read the output before and after the fix.
try: Compare the first output with the three rows in the file. Find the group that was left off the page. Add ("Lab","") to the list and run the script again. Count the printed rows.
after: The first version skips HR. The fixed output includes Ops Lead A, HR UNASSIGNED and Docs Lead B. The final report has four rows. Lab UNASSIGNED comes last.
why: Printing a blank label is different from dropping the whole item. The reader still needs to see that the group exists.
rescue: If a group disappears, look for a line that prints only when the owner has text. Move printing outside that check.

premise: Turn a repeated writing job into a skill. A skill is a small set of directions the tool can reuse.
before:
Change: export now keeps empty departments.
Evidence: 4 sample rows passed.
try: Open the skill file in the folder. Read its directions and check that they name the input and output files. Start a new session here and enter /note. Change the source evidence to say 6 sample rows passed. Save it and run /note again.
after: The recipe is in .claude/skills/note/SKILL.md. The source says four sample rows passed. The second note still has two headings. It now says six rows passed.
why: A reusable recipe should read the ingredients on the counter each time. Facts in the old note do not belong in the new one.
rescue: If the slash command is missing, check the folder, file name and skill name. Start a fresh session in that folder.

premise: Compare a current list with a wanted list. Show who would be added, kept or removed without changing a real group.
before: {"current":[" Sand ","BLUE","blue","Gray"],"desired":["sand","Gold","","GOLD"]}
try: Run the preview. Draw two circles on paper for current and wanted. Write an item in the middle if it is in both. Replace desired with an exact copy of current. Run the same command and read all three lists.
after: Add gold. Remove blue and gray. Keep sand. Keep blue, gray and sand. The add and remove lists are both empty.
why: A preview is a shopping list of possible changes. You can check it before any real change is allowed.
rescue: If BLUE and blue get split, ask the code to clean both input lists before comparing them.

premise: Two rules disagree on a single day. Find that day and show which readers it affects.
before:
V1: members ALLOW. Guests ALLOW when days < 7; otherwise REVIEW.
V2: members ALLOW. Guests ALLOW when days <= 7; otherwise REVIEW.
Only member and guest are in scope.
try: Circle the < and <= signs in the source. Use the table to find the guest row where one rule includes day seven. Ask Claude to count every changed row in the four test cases. Look at the two rows for day eight yourself.
after: A day-seven guest changes from REVIEW to ALLOW. A day-six guest is allowed by both. There is one change. At day eight both versions review guests and allow members.
why: A one-character edit can change access for someone right at a boundary. Checking a day on either side shows the size of the change.
rescue: If all guests are allowed on day eight, read the guest and member branches separately. Use the row labels when you compare.

premise: A pretend directory has three pages, including an empty middle page. Collect every item and catch a broken link.
before: {"one":{"items":["M1","M2"],"next":"two"},"two":{"items":[],"next":"three"},"three":{"items":["M2","M3"],"next":null}}
try: Open the middle page in the file. It has no items but it does name a next page. Run the reader on the unchanged sample. Replace the last null with "one" and run it. Replace that with "absent" and run it again.
after: It prints ["M1","M2","M3"]. M2 appears only once. The first change reports a loop. The second reports a missing page. Neither prints a partial result as a success.
why: A book can have a blank page between two full ones. Following its page arrows finds the last chapter.
rescue: If it stops after M2, look at the rule for ending the loop. Only a missing next link marked null ends the normal run.

premise: Freeze the clock for a test. Find out which items expire at midnight and which expire one second later.
try: Look for Z at the end of each time. It marks the same clock for every row. Compare each deadline with the first test time. Run the same two checks twice. Ask Claude to show how many items have expired at each check time.
after: At midnight A and B have expired. C remains active for one more second. Two expire at midnight and all three at 00:00:01Z, every time you run the test.
why: A fixed clock is like pausing a video on the same frame. You can check an exact instant tomorrow as easily as today.
rescue: If the answer changes with today's date, pass the fixed time into the rule. Replace any call that reads the current clock inside the test.

premise: Save rows one at a time. Reopen the saved file after a forced stop and make sure repeats add no points.
before:
id,amount
E1,4
E2,8
E1,4
E3,5
try: Stop after two rows. Read the saved list. Restart with the same file. Compare that result with a fresh run on an empty database. Append E2,99 to the input. Run it again with the saved database. Ask for the stored value of E2.
after: The stop leaves E1 and E2, total 12. Restart adds E3 and the total is 17. E2 is still 8. The three IDs still total 17.
why: For this importer, the first slip with an ID wins. A later copy cannot change a score that was already saved.
rescue: If the total grows on each run, check that the database stores the ID as a unique key. Run twice on the same file to prove it.

premise: Save a new version of a small address book. Prove you can turn the new file back into the original data.
before: [{"id":1,"address":"a@example.test","note":"A, B"},{"id":2,"address":null,"note":""},{"id":3,"address":"b@c@example.test","note":"x"}]
try: Run the two scripts. Open the row containing two @ signs. Find which one split the address. Look at the row that has a blank note. Run both steps again. Compare the data in roundtrip.json with the untouched original, including the comma in a note.
after: The new file has three rows in the original order. The missing address is still null. Every ID, address, note and position matches. Different spacing around the JSON text does not change a value.
why: A return trip is a strong test. If even a comma inside a note goes missing, the trip did not carry everything back.
rescue: If an address changes, split at the last @. Keep null as its own value rather than writing the word null as a string.

premise: Practice reading a result before scoring a tool. This made-up example could come from any builder.
before: The first game opens at Blue 0, Gold 0. Blue gets Question 1 right. The first tap shows Blue 2, Gold 0.
try: Tap the same choice again straight away. Look at both totals, the question number and the active team. Finish the game and check the other four rules on the page.
after: Suppose the second tap changes Blue to 4. Mark the click-lock check Fail and record both scores. If all four other checks pass, the first-try score is 4 out of 5.
why: Two taps on one answer count as just one pick. The number on the screen lets another reader repeat your check.
rescue: If the screen changes too fast to tell, restart and repeat the double tap. Leave the check untested until you can tell what happened. Keep this first file when you try the later edit.

premise: The first two items are free. Catch the new code charging for the second item and give a friend a way to check the fix.
before:
Contract: first two items free. Each additional item costs 1.25 dollars. Whole nonnegative counts only. Use fixed two-decimal amounts. Reject negatives.
Previous formula: max(0,n-2)*1.25
Candidate formula: max(0,n-1)*1.25
try: Run the tests on the candidate before changing it. Try two items. Save what the wrong rule charges. Then repair it and run the tests again. Run the command from evidence.md yourself. Try six items and then -1. Read the price or error each time.
after: The first program fails at two items. The fixed rule charges 0.00 for zero or two items, and 1.25 for three. Six costs 5.00. A negative count is rejected. A new reader can repeat the same checks.
why: An answer key copied from a broken program will repeat its mistake. A printed rule gives you an independent way to judge the result.
rescue: If the bad code passes all tests, add the exact last free item to the test table. Check the expected price before running it.

premise: Mail A and mail B joined the same queue. Find out which one reached the end.
before:
A queued
B queued
A retrying
A delivered
try: Number the four lines on paper. Circle the last A and the last B. Compare those two circles with the line numbers in the reply. Add B delivered on line 5 and save. Ask Codex to read the file again.
after: A was delivered on line 4. B was queued on line 2. B is now delivered on line 5. A still points to line 4.
why: A log is like a diary. Read its entries in order. A missing delivery line means we do not yet know what happened next.
rescue: If B is marked failed, ask to see the exact line that says failed.

premise: Make a little book that flips between two things to check.
before:
Check queue
Verify delivery
try: Open index.html in your browser. Check the title and the count together. Set a finger on Next and see how far you can go from page 1. Click Next, try Next again, then click Previous.
after: The browser starts on Check queue, 1 of 2. Previous is off. Page 2 says Verify delivery, 2 of 2. Next is off. Previous takes you back to page 1.
why: The count tells the reader where they are. A button at the last page should never open a made-up third page.
rescue: If code appears as text, check that the file ends in .html and open it in a browser.

premise: Count how many rounds each team played and how many points each kept.
before:
player,points
Blue,80
Gold,35
Blue,-75
Gold,0
Blue,10
try: Make two piles on paper, one per team. Blue has 80 - 75 + 10. Gold has 35 + 0. Count the slips as well as the points. Add Gold,-40 on a new line. Save the file and run python3 totals.py again.
after: Blue played 3 rounds for 15 points. Gold played 2 rounds for 35 points. Gold now has 3 rounds and -5 points. Blue stays at 15.
why: A zero is a score someone entered. A minus takes points away. Neither one erases a round.
rescue: If Gold has only one round at the start, look for a rule that skips a zero.

premise: Leave rules in the project so a fresh chat knows how to write a findings file.
before: Every findings file is a JSON array. Each item has exactly two keys: id and status. The status is uppercase. Sort items by id ascending. Omit commentary inside JSON.
try: Open both JSON files in a text editor. Count the fields in each row. Lower and uppercase letters matter in this rule. Start a fresh Codex chat in this same folder. Ask for second-findings.json using Z9 closed and B2 open. Leave out the rules this time.
after: The first file lists A1 OPEN and A2 CLOSED. Each row has just id and status. B2 OPEN comes before Z9 CLOSED. The same two fields appear.
why: A project rule card works like the rules inside a game box. A new player can use them without the last player there.
rescue: If the second file has extra fields, check that the fresh task opened the folder holding AGENTS.md.

premise: Two exports can list the same entry. Pick the newest one and catch ties that disagree.
before:
id,rev,label
x,2,New
y,1,First
x,1,Old
y,1,First
try: Sort the x rows by their revision numbers. Cross off the older one. The two equal y rows can share one spot. Save a copy of merged.csv. Add x,2,Conflict to the input and run the tool again. Compare both output files.
after: merged.csv has x,2,New and y,1,First below the header. The tool reports the tie. The last good merged.csv still matches its copy.
why: Numbers on the rows work like edition numbers on a book. Two different texts labeled with the same edition need a person to check them.
rescue: If the tie silently picks the last row, ask for a check before the tool writes its output.

premise: A reader wants to find mail topics even if they type capitals or stray spaces.
before:
Mailbox Review
Group Audit
Mail Flow
Archive Plan
try: Type MAIL with one space on either side in the web page. Read the displayed titles, then compare the number beside the box. Try xyz. Then erase the whole search, including spaces.
after: Searching for MAIL with spaces on either side finds Mailbox Review and Mail Flow. The count is 2. The screen shows 0 matches for xyz. The empty field brings back all four titles.
why: An empty search asks to see everything. A real word with no match asks for an empty list.
rescue: If only Mail Flow appears, ask for matches anywhere inside a title. Mailbox counts too.

premise: A limit of five should still let someone in when the count is exactly five.
before:
def allowed(count):
    return count <= 5
try: Write three columns marked 4, 5 and 6. Under each, write what <= 5 means. Try the same columns for < 5. Ask for the smallest repair. Run the function with 4, 5 and 6 before the repair and again after it.
after: The saved rule allows 5. The changed rule stops it. Four still passes and six still fails. The repaired answers, in order, are True, True and False.
why: The little equal sign includes the number on the fence. Tests far away from five would miss this mistake.
rescue: If no change appears, save the original <= file in Git first. Then change only <= to < in your working file.

premise: A program needs exact fields each time so it can open both answers.
before: {"type":"object","properties":{"sent":{"type":"integer"},"held":{"type":"integer"},"unknown":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["sent","held","unknown"],"additionalProperties":false}
try: Circle sent twice and held once in the first request. Compare each count with the value next to the same name in result.json. Run the command again. Replace the list inside the quoted request with held, held. Use second.json as the output name.
after: result.json contains sent 2, held 1 and unknown 1. The second file contains sent 0, held 2 and unknown 0, with no extra fields.
why: Think of the field rules as three labeled cups. Each state goes into its cup. An empty cup has a count of zero.
rescue: If the terminal cannot find codex, finish its command-line setup first. If the shape is wrong, check the file after the -o option.

premise: A person needs counts. The example addresses and message text can stay in the input file.
before:
email,status,message
one@example.test,OK,reviewed
two@example.test,,pending
three@example.test,ok,reviewed
try: Open the report as plain text. Search it for the @ sign and a word from a sample message before you share the counts. Add four@example.test,OK,contact-me to audit.csv. Run the script again. Search summary.json for @, contact-me and example.test.
after: The first counts are ok 2, unknown 1 and total 3. The new counts are ok 3, unknown 1 and total 4. None of the three search terms appears.
why: You can count envelopes without copying the address on each one. Check the file people will receive.
rescue: If you see an address in the output, find the step that copies whole rows. Keep just the count fields.

premise: Pretend that a service asks you to wait twice. Count your tries without contacting a real service.
before: [{"status":429,"retry_after":2},{"status":429,"retry_after":4},{"status":200,"items":["G1"]}]
try: Write a row for each attempt. Put a wait between tries one and two and between two and three. There is no space for a wait after the third. Change the final reply to {"status":429,"retry_after":8}. Run the same program.
after: You get G1 on try 3. The planned waits are 2 and 4. The tool stops after three tries. It still lists only 2 and 4 for waits, since there is no fourth try.
why: A shop may ask you to come back later. When you have used your last try, waiting again cannot help.
rescue: If 8 appears in the second list, move the wait step behind the check for a try still left.

premise: An old game called its points score. A newer save calls the same value points.
before: [{"v":1,"name":"Blue","score":-5},{"v":2,"name":"Gold","points":0},{"v":3,"name":"Future","points":10}]
try: Open the output after each save. Mark whether its points field is present, then read its value. Zero passes both checks. Load v2 successfully. Copy current.json to a second file. Try loading v3 and compare the files.
after: Version 1 restores Blue at -5 points. Version 2 restores Gold at 0. The tool reports an unknown version. Every byte of the saved Gold result is unchanged.
why: A new label can still describe the same number. A version the tool has never seen is different: it has no instructions for reading it.
rescue: If zero becomes a default, check whether the field exists. A number can be zero and still be present.

premise: Members can get permission through a group inside another group. Draw the path so you can see why each permission appears.
before: {"Blue":["Editors","Readers"],"Editors":["Readers","permit:write"],"Readers":["Editors","permit:read"],"Gold":[]}
try: Draw arrows from Blue to both groups. Cross off a group as soon as you enter it. List only the permit labels you reach. Add permit:read directly to Blue as another arrow. Run access.py again for both teams.
after: Blue reaches permit:read and permit:write once each. Gold reaches neither. Blue still has two different permissions. Every path printed can be traced through the input.
why: Think of checking rooms in a maze. Once a room is checked, another door into it cannot add a new room by itself.
rescue: If the program keeps running, make sure it records a visit before following the next arrow.

premise: Several jobs can run together. Work out the largest number running at once.
before:
id,start,end
A,0,3
B,2,4
C,3,5
D,3,3
try: Draw five one-minute boxes in a row. Shade a job on each minute it uses. Count the marks in each column. Change A to start 0 and end 2. Run again. Then give every job the same end as its own start.
after: Two jobs first run together at minute 2. The peak is still 2, now first seen at minute 3. With no running time, the count is 0 and there is no busiest minute.
why: When one job stops at minute 3, its spot is free for a job starting at 3. It cannot take both spots.
rescue: If three jobs appear at minute 3, look for an end minute that was counted as part of the job.

premise: Practice reading a result before scoring a tool. This made-up example could come from any builder.
before: The first game opens at Blue 0, Gold 0. Blue gets Question 1 right. The first tap shows Blue 2, Gold 0.
try: Tap the same choice again straight away. Look at both totals, the question number and the active team. Finish the game and check the other four rules on the page.
after: Suppose the second tap changes Blue to 4. Mark the click-lock check Fail and record both scores. If all four other checks pass, the first-try score is 4 out of 5.
why: Two taps on one answer count as just one pick. The number on the screen lets another reader repeat your check.
rescue: If the screen changes too fast to tell, restart and repeat the double tap. Leave the check untested until you can tell what happened. Keep this first file when you try the later edit.

premise: Build a report someone else can run and check from a short set of directions.
before:
id,status
A,OK
B,HOLD
B,HOLD
C,OK
try: Open README.md from the new folder. Follow its instructions as if you had never seen the chat. Compare the printed counts to the source rows. Keep a copy of the good output. Add C,HOLD and try again. Next use a fresh file with just the header and run the test command from the README.
after: The good report says ok 2, hold 1 and total 3. The conflict fails and keeps the good file. A header alone gives 0, 0, 0. All tests pass.
why: A clear handover lets another person prove the tool works without borrowing your chat history.
rescue: If a duplicate counts twice, compare IDs before adding up the states. Save the output after all rows pass.

premise: Which of six pretend mailboxes should appear on a list for people and shared teams? You can build the report without connecting to a mail system.
before: Six rows: two shared mailboxes, two user mailboxes, one room and one device. The output begins with the address accounts@example.test.
try: Sort the four included addresses by hand. Open your CSV with Import-Csv and tick them off in that order. Then run the supplied tests. Run the kit tests. Try the temporary copy that sorts backward. Run the tests again with the original answer file.
after: The four addresses sort as accounts@example.test, box-a@example.test, box-b@example.test and box-c@example.test. The types in order are shared, user, shared, user. All five checks pass with the original. The backward sort fails. Team, Blue stays in one name field and Café Desk keeps its accent. Room and device rows stay out.
why: A test with pretend mailboxes can find a broken report before it touches a real service. A pretend live read only checks your script’s behavior.
rescue: If four rows appear but the order is wrong, open the CSV with Import-Csv and check the sorted address field.

premise: A mailbox gets a watch label at 80%. Try the number just below it, the number itself and the one above.
try: Look at the little equals sign. Put 79, 80 and 81 on a number line and mark everything at or above 80 as watch. Run label(-1) as a separate trial. Discuss whether the word normal makes sense for that input.
after: 79 is normal. Both 80 and 81 are watch. The current code returns normal. You have found a missing rule for a bad percentage.
why: Checking both sides of a fence shows which side the fence post belongs on.
rescue: If 80 is labeled normal, look for > where the sample says >=.

premise: A team label contains a comma. The table should still have just two columns.
before:
sample.csv:
id,name
m1,"North, West"
m2,East
parser.py starter: print([len(line.rstrip().split(",")) for line in open("sample.csv")])
try: Put a pencil loop around the quotes on the m1 row. Draw a line only at the comma outside those quotes. You should see two fields. Add m3,"" as a new row. Check its two fields and see whether the second field stays empty.
after: The broken count list is 2, 3, 2. The fixed list is 2, 2, 2. The new row has two fields. The second is an empty string. North, West stays together on its own row.
why: In a CSV file, quotes can wrap a comma that belongs inside a single field.
rescue: If North and West still show up as separate columns, see whether the script still splits each line by hand.

premise: A report should find its own sample table even if you open a terminal somewhere else.
before:
site,count
West,3
East,5
try: Run the report from the folder above cleanlab. Read the input path if it fails. Check which folder really contains rows.csv. Copy the named files into a fresh folder. Run there. Then try a separate copy with the input missing.
after: From inside cleanlab, python3 report.py prints 8. From one folder above, python3 cleanlab/report.py also prints 8. Both complete copies print 8. The copy missing its input stops with an error.
why: A street address for a file can start at the script or at the terminal. This tool needs the script’s folder.
rescue: If the second command cannot find rows.csv, ask how the script builds the path to that file.

premise: A list has stray spaces and two spellings of the same ID. Find the one ID in the noise.
try: Write each ID surrounded by brackets so you can see the spaces. Clean the labels before using a list of items already seen. Try B2 and b2 with outside spaces, plus two spellings of C3. Also test an empty list.
after: The supplied list should give just a1. Before the repair extra spaces create extra entries. The new group gives b2 and c3 once each. The empty group gives an empty list.
why: Clean each label before checking whether you have seen it. A string of spaces becomes empty after cleaning.
rescue: If you cannot see the spaces, ask Python to print repr for each item so its edges show.

premise: Leave a short recipe for checking a count sheet. Try it on a second sheet without explaining it all over again.
before:
ID,Count
a,3
b,0
c,
try: Cross out negative, blank and broken counts. Include zero in the row count and write zero in the sum. Compare your paper rule with the recipe. Open a fresh session and give it only the recipe and the second sheet with x=-2, y=8 and z=1.
after: Rows a and b are valid, even though b is zero. Their sum is 3. Row c needs a look. Two rows count. The sum is 9. Row x needs a look.
why: A clear recipe works on new numbers. A recipe that just remembers the first answer cannot pass this test.
rescue: If b disappears, add a line to the recipe showing that zero is a real count.

premise: A tiny scorecard is only useful if it remembers your points when you reopen the page.
before: Start 0. Add 12. Add -5. Reload the page. Submit a blank field.
try: Record the score before each click, after each click and after reload. Add a separate line for the blank field, which should leave the total alone. Submit a blank entry. Read the hint. Reload the same address once more.
after: The total starts at 0, then becomes 12, then 7. Reload shows 7. The total stays 7 both times. The hint asks for a number.
why: The saved number works like a bookmark. The same browser at the same address can find it later.
rescue: If reload starts from zero, check whether the tool reads its saved value when it opens, before drawing the score.

premise: A ticket desk received the same card several times. The second revision really is a new task.
before:
delivery,issue,revision
d1,T21,r1
d1,T21,r1
d2,T21,r1
d3,T21,r2
try: Make a paper card for each different issue and revision. Check the stored tasks after a restart against those cards. Run the first three rows, close the program, then run the full list with the same database. Add d4,T22,r1.
after: The four events produce two tasks: T21/r1 and T21/r2. Old deliveries keep their tasks after restart. The new issue makes the third task.
why: Think of a pair as a two-part locker number. You need both parts to know which locker is yours.
rescue: If a restart makes extra tasks, check that both runs open the same database file and use the same two-part match.

premise: Compare the approved list with what the test report actually found. Check both directions.
before:
Approved: Reader/reports, Maintainer/app.
Observed: Reader/reports, Reader/reports, Reader/app.
try: Write two columns, approved and observed. Cross out each matching pair once. A second copy of the same pair gets a separate repeat mark. Replace the repeat Reader/reports with Maintainer/app and remove Reader/app. Run again.
after: Reader/app is extra. Maintainer/app is missing. Reader/reports is repeated. The lists now match. The repeat also disappears.
why: If you check only for extra keys, you may miss a key someone should have received.
rescue: If the missing pair is absent from the report, compare approved against observed in a separate pass.

premise: Several sessions can work on the same change. Count that change once when you measure the cost.
before:
session,units,pr,accepted
s1,4,P1,yes
s2,2,P1,yes
s3,3,P2,no
s4,1,,no
try: Add all four unit charges, including failed work. Circle the ID P1 once. Divide by the number of different accepted IDs you circled. Set every accepted marker to no and repeat the report.
after: The rows use 10 units. Only P1 is accepted. That gives 10 units per accepted change. Total use is still 10. Accepted changes are 0. The rate has no value because you cannot divide by zero.
why: A second receipt for work on the same job still costs something. It does not turn that job into two finished jobs.
rescue: If you get 5 units per win, check whether you counted two yes rows for P1.

premise: Two events both say 1:15. Their offsets show that they happened an hour apart.
try: Add four hours to the first 01:15 and five hours to the next 01:15. Read their new positions against the test window. Move only the start to 05:15:01 UTC. Run the same checks.
after: A is 05:15 UTC and B is 06:15 UTC. Both count. C is exactly at the end. D has no offset. Now only B is in the window. The gap from A to B is still 60 minutes.
why: The offset tells you how to compare a clock with UTC. Two clocks can both show 1:15 at different moments.
rescue: If C is counted, change the test for the end time from at or before to strictly before.

premise: A pretend service makes a task but the “done” message never arrives. Should you make another?
before:
Create T9: store S1, then throw timeout.
Lookup T9: one match S1.
Create call counter begins at zero.
try: Stop after the pretend service stores S1 but before a reply arrives. Reopen the client. Inspect the saved tag and count actual create calls. Change the lookup so T9 has both S1 and S2. Try the check again.
after: One match returns S1. The create count is 1, even after restart. The result says which two IDs conflict. It makes no new task.
why: A lost receipt does not prove a job was lost. Look for the job before paying for a second one.
rescue: If the second run creates a task, check that it reads the saved unknown result before it tries to start anything.

premise: An app is changing count to total. Update the reader before you update the writer.
try: Draw a box around each key in the two-field example. Compare their values. Accept that row only if both ways of reading it agree. Put the old writer back and keep the new reader. Read its output once more.
after: The old record, the new record and the equal pair each give 2. The mismatched pair fails. The old record still gives 2. The reader still rejects count 2 paired with total 3.
why: Teaching the reader both words first gives the writer time to change. It also gives you a way back.
rescue: If the reader chooses one number from a conflicting pair, add the check for two fields before choosing either one.

premise: A two-team report is missing half its data. Keep yesterday’s good total until you have a full new one.
before:
current.json contains {"total":7}
manifest: North,South
partial input: North=4
good input: North=4,South=5
try: Make a spare copy of current.json. Stop the new write just before the report swap. Compare the visible report with your spare. Run with North=4 and South=5. Then try two North rows and no South.
after: A file naming only North leaves 7. A forced stop with both rows ready also leaves the old file exactly as it was. The full set writes 9. The bad repeat leaves that good 9 unchanged.
why: A spare sheet lets you finish and check your work before you replace the copy other people are reading.
rescue: If the old report vanishes, check whether the program opens it for writing before all the checks finish.

premise: A group wants a yes or no before a move. It needs a full count and a real approval.
before: Manifest North,South. R1 North 48/50. R2 South 47/50. A1 owner: review pending.
try: Use two marks: one for 95 of 100 and one for owner approval. Both must be present. Check each group exists before doing the addition. Change A1 to approved. Then separately test missing South and a restored South at 51/50. Follow the README in a fresh folder.
after: The starting numbers are 95 of 100, but A1 says review pending. The result is HOLD. Approval makes the complete set pass at exactly 95%. Both bad sets stop, and the test directions work for the next reader.
why: A high score cannot fill a missing row or sign a permission slip. All three pieces of proof matter.
rescue: If 51/50 gives a pass, compare completed with attempted for each group before adding the groups.

premise: A board game starts at 4. You want to arrive a little early. Can the helper keep two time rules in mind?
before: The walk takes 10 minutes. Players need 5 minutes to set up before 4.
try: Ask when to leave. Request a little timeline. Add “The walk now takes 15 minutes” in a fresh try.
after: First leave at 3:45. Then leave at 3:40. Both trips end at 3:55, in time to set up.
why: Changing the walk should change the start of the walk. The game still starts at 4.
rescue: If the answer says 3:50, point out the five minutes of setup. Try a higher thinking level and check the clock again.

premise: Your tiny app reads flyers and fills two boxes. What should it do when a flyer leaves a box empty?
before: Flyer one says “Game Day, June 4.” Flyer two says “Game Day.” The app has Title and Date boxes.
try: Test two model IDs from the chapter using both flyers. Ask for just Title and Date. Write down each result.
after: Both titles say Game Day. Only the first flyer gets a date. The second date is empty or null.
why: One missing fact makes a better test than two perfectly neat flyers. You can see whether the helper makes up a date.
rescue: If both dates match, submit the second flyer alone in a fresh request. Say to use null when the source has no date.

premise: A game-night flyer needs a start time. Two notes disagree.
before: Draft says Game Night starts at 6. Final says it starts at 7.
try: Select Final alone. Ask for the start time and open its citation. In Studio, make a one-page infographic for players. Read the time printed on it.
after: Final gives 7. A flyer showing 7 passes this check. One showing 6 needs a fresh output.
why: A source proves where the time came from. Checking the picture catches errors that can slip in after a correct chat answer.
rescue: Open Final and read the line yourself. Clear Draft and generate the flyer again if it shows the old time.

premise: A player wants a game that asks one riddle and tells them whether their guess is right.
before: The riddle is “What has keys and plays music?” The practice answer is piano.
try: In AI Studio Build, ask for one question, an answer box and a Check button. Ask it to ignore case and spaces at the ends. Open the preview.
after: “piano” and “ PIANO ” both win. “drum” gives a hint. A blank guess asks the player to type first.
why: Three different tries give you a way to tell a working game from a nice-looking screen.
rescue: If pressing Check always says “correct,” show the tool the drum test and ask it to fix the check. Play all three cases again.

premise: You want a title screen with a picture and a short welcome sound. Each needs its own check.
before: The picture should show one gold key on blue cloth. The spoken words should be “Find the key.”
try: Make the still picture first. Keep space for the title. Give the exact welcome line to a speech tool. Play the result and count the words you hear.
after: There is one key, room for the title and one clear spoken line of three words.
why: The picture and the sound do separate jobs. Checking the words in the recording catches a line that looks right on screen but sounds wrong.
rescue: If the voice says “gold key,” paste the exact three-word line again. Add the final title as editable text above the picture.

premise: A reusable project helps a volunteer answer the same pretend park-fee question next week.
before: Rate card says $2 per hour on weekdays and $3 per hour on weekends. One event note says game day costs $8 for the visit.
try: Put both files in a Claude Project. Ask what two hours cost on an ordinary Saturday. Then say the Saturday is game day and ask again.
after: The ordinary Saturday costs $6. The game-day visit costs $8. Each answer should name the file that supplies its rule.
why: The event note changes the whole visit. The reader needs to see when that special rule applies.
rescue: If both answers say $6, ask to quote the event note. Check that the file belongs to the project and that the second question mentions game day.

premise: You want the fastest choice that still follows a rule when a message sounds urgent.
before: Two pretend notes read “Locked out of mail” and “Urgent: change the room sign.” The labels are Mail and Other.
try: Try the same two notes with two models from the chapter. Ask for exactly one label per note. Cover the model names and score the answers first.
after: The first label is Mail. The second is Other. A tidy answer with the wrong second label earns only one point.
why: The urgent wording is a distraction. A correct answer follows the subject of the note.
rescue: If the second note is labeled Mail, write a clearer label rule, then run both models again with the same revised prompt.

premise: Your app lists four books, and its date filter must keep old links working.
before: Two books have June 1 dates, one is June 2 and one has no date. An old link opens the third book.
try: Ask Claude Code to plan a filter before editing. Try June 1, June 3, then Clear. Open the saved link.
after: You see two books, then zero, then all four. The old link still opens the same book.
why: Testing the clear button catches a common mistake: quietly dropping the book that has no date.
rescue: If only three books return, point out the blank date. Ask the tool to run its clear-filter test using all four sample books.

premise: Two notice pages give opening hours. You want an answer checked against each open page.
before: The first public sample page says Saturday 10–4. The second says Saturday 12–5.
try: Use a supported Chrome side panel to read each page. Ask for the hours and the title of the page that gave them. Check the originals.
after: The table keeps 10–4 with the first page and 12–5 with the second. Both rows identify their source.
why: A helper can easily repeat the active tab twice. Different times make that easy to spot.
rescue: If both rows say 10–4, share the second tab and ask about that tab alone before rebuilding the comparison.

premise: You need a player to see the direction of travel on a small screen.
before: The design calls for one thick arrow pointing right. The background should have no decorative marks.
try: Ask Claude for an SVG arrow. Open the result beside the chat as an Artifact. Shrink the view to about the size of a game button.
after: The point is on the right and still easy to see. The rest of the drawing does not cover the arrow.
why: A drawing that is clear at full size can be hard to read on the button a player will press.
rescue: If the arrow looks like a line, ask for a wider head and a thicker stem. Reopen the revised SVG at the same small size.

premise: A public post says boarding changed. You need to know whether a change applies to every sailing.
before: Practice with a pretend notice: “Saturday trial only. Boarding opens at noon on route A.”
try: Ask which day, route and start time the words support. If researching a real notice, find the operator’s own post and open the exact link.
after: You can say Saturday, route A, noon. Nothing in the sample gives a weekday time or a time for route B.
why: Finding the real post is only half the job. Its words set limits on the claim.
