rescue: If an answer says all routes changed, underline “route A” and ask for one new sentence limited to the notice.

premise: A public guide lists early closing on one date. You want the time for that date only.
before: Practice calendar: “Ordinary Saturdays: closes at 5. Special Saturday: closes at 3.”
try: Ask for the special-day time and a sentence that backs it. In live search, open the source and read the row for the date in question.
after: The answer is 3. A link to the ordinary hours alone gives the wrong answer for this day.
why: A source can be official but still cover a different day. Look for a match between the question and the cited row.
rescue: If the answer says 5, ask it to find the exception. Repeat the check with the event calendar open in Comet.

premise: You want a small AI helper to answer a new question away from the internet.
before: Your computer already has a compatible local model and the app that runs it. A saved practice note says “Blue tokens score four.”
try: Disconnect from the network and restart the local app. Give it the saved note and ask how many points two blue tokens are worth.
after: The app answers eight and can point to the four-point rule. Try changing the note to three per token. The new answer should be six.
why: The second question tests a fresh calculation. Replaying a saved answer would miss the changed rule.
rescue: If the app asks to connect, check that the model and required files finished downloading before the offline test.

premise: A reader is unsure which of two open tabs a helper used.
before: Tab one lists an adult ticket for $8. Tab two lists a child ticket for $3. Both examples are invented.
try: Share only the first tab and ask for both prices. Next explicitly share the second tab and repeat the request.
after: In the first run the child price lacks a source. With both tabs shared, you can check $8 and $3 against their own pages.
why: The visible input explains why an answer changed. It also lets you limit the pages a helper can read.
rescue: If the answer invents a child price in the first run, ask for the exact words. Mark any price without support as unknown.

premise: You want an assistant to spot a sign that changes in a short animation.
before: The sign reads WAIT at the start, GO for one second in the middle and WAIT at the end.
try: Give the full clip to a tool that reads video. Give only the first and last pictures to a tool that reads still images. Ask when the sign says GO.
after: A full-clip answer can be checked against the middle second. The two stills show no GO frame and cannot establish when it appeared.
why: Two different inputs make this a test of the tools you supplied. Use matching evidence for a fair model comparison.
rescue: If the still-picture answer guesses a time, ask it to point to the picture that supports the guess. Add the middle frame and repeat.

premise: A model gives low-cost replies, yet several need another try. Can the cheaper reply still cost more per success?
before: In a pretend trial, helper A costs 12 cents for 4 checked answers. Helper B costs 15 cents for 10.
try: Divide the full bill for each helper by the number of answers you can use. Include the attempts that failed in the bill.
after: A costs 3 cents per good answer. B costs 1.5 cents per good answer.
why: The price of one message and the price of solving the job answer different questions.
rescue: If you compare 12 with 15 alone, add a second column for checked answers. Mark which units belong in the top and bottom of each sum.

premise: Your app needs a printed card as well as a small picture on its home screen.
before: The print is 6 inches wide by 4 inches high. The requested print quality is 300 pixels per inch.
try: Multiply 6 by 300 for width and 4 by 300 for height. Look at the exported image details. Then view a smaller copy at actual button size.
after: The print file has at least 1,800 by 1,200 pixels. The icon still shows its main shape when small.
why: A large file can print well but look busy as an icon. Each use needs its own check.
rescue: If the print is 600 by 400, a larger preview on screen changes nothing. Export enough pixels from the original artwork.

premise: Three helpers give different answers about an evening fee. You can settle it with the rule.
before: Started hours cost $2, up to $10. A visit that starts at 6 p.m. or later costs $4. A car arrives at 5:30 and leaves at 7:45.
try: Ask each helper for the fee and the words that set it. Then change only “starts” to “ends” and ask again.
after: The first rule gives $6 for three started hours. With the changed rule, the evening exit makes the fee $4.
why: The same minutes can have two correct prices under two different rules. A good explanation points to the changed word.
rescue: If it gives $4 both times, ask for the arrival time and the exit time on separate lines before applying the rule.

premise: The mail report prints a dash for a missing score and for a real zero. A reader cannot tell them apart.
before: One sample row contains 0, one contains a blank and a third contains 5.
try: Start Ask in the training project. Ask which file turns these values into display text. Open its cited line. If you need an edit, pass the three rows to Agent.
after: A report that follows the rule shows 0, a dash and 5 in the same order.
why: A small example tells the helper when the job is done. It also tells you when to stop at reading the file.
rescue: If both of the first two rows still show a dash, give the two separate expected results and ask for a test that includes both.

premise: The practice mail report has an empty day. Someone asks whether the file will still have column names. The review is due before the team leaves.
before: Open the Exchange inventory kit from Devin lab 1. The folder has a made-up mailbox list, a test file and a Reference folder with the finished script.
try: Ask Devin which test checks an empty day in the saved project. Open the line it cites in Test-Inventory.ps1. Then use the terminal in the kit folder to run pwsh -File ./Test-Inventory.ps1 -Script ./Reference/Get-MailboxInventory.ps1.
after: Five PASS lines appear. The second says “empty input retains its header.” That line checks the case in the question. A teammate can repeat the same command.
why: Ask found the rule without starting a cloud Agent. Running the test showed how this copy acts. If the team later asks for a fix that must run after you leave, a prepared cloud session can use the same check.
rescue: If the terminal cannot find the test file, open the folder that contains Test-Inventory.ps1. If it cannot find pwsh, use a computer with PowerShell 7 or ask the setup owner to add it to the Blueprint and rebuild.

premise: A library help page has a clear rule, but its final line got lost in a draft.
before: The rule permits one renewal if nobody is waiting. The current draft says only that one renewal is allowed.
try: Use Ask to find the source page. Give Agent the full rule, ask for one changed sentence and open the new page using the old link.
after: The page says one renewal is allowed if nobody is waiting. Its old address still works.
why: A page can load correctly and still say the wrong thing. Check meaning and navigation separately.
rescue: If the new text appears only in a generated copy, ask which source file builds it, make the change there and generate the page again.

premise: A test runs in an old session. Does the team’s saved setup include everything the test needs?
before: The old session had a tool installed by hand. A clean session contains only what the setup recipe includes.
try: Start a fresh practice session. Ask it for the tool version and run one known test. If the command is missing, inspect the recipe and repeat on another fresh session after fixing it.
after: Both a new session and its successor can find the tool and pass the same test.
why: A test that only works on one computer can give the next reader a false sense of success.
rescue: If it still passes only on the old machine, record the folder and version from both. Look for a step that was done by hand.

premise: A game receives the same scoring event twice when its connection comes back.
before: A7 gives 3 points. B8 also gives 3. The game receives A7, B8 and A7 again.
try: Ask Devin to trace the total in a read-only session. Then ask Agent for a test with those three events. Read the expected total before it edits the game.
after: After each arrival, the scores are 3, 6 and 6. Two different IDs with equal amounts both count.
why: The ID describes the event. The score amount alone cannot tell which turn was repeated.
rescue: If the total is 3, the fix probably discarded B8 because it also scored 3. Show the two IDs and test again.

premise: A review shows green checks, but you need to know whether the newest change actually passed them.
before: The old test ran on version A. The file changed afterward, making version B.
try: Open the review’s file list. Compare the version reported by the last test with the version the reviewer is about to accept. On B, repeat the same event twice.
after: The test and the review both name B. Repeating the event adds one stored row and one charge.
why: A passing check on A tells you what happened before the latest edit. It cannot check the new line.
rescue: If the versions differ, ask for a fresh test on B. Keep the older result as a record, then link the new one.

premise: A teammate should be able to repeat your check without guessing which folder or rule you used.
before: Your practice skill requires an importer name, a version and a written rule for repeat IDs.
try: Try the skill once with all three inputs. Try it again in a fresh session with the repeat rule left out. Read the final record from each run.
after: The first run shows the expected and actual total. The second asks for the missing rule before editing.
why: Asking a good question is a correct result when the skill lacks a required fact.
rescue: If both sessions guess at the rule, move the missing-input check to the first step of the skill. Repeat using another fresh session.

premise: A ticket board delivers one event twice, then sends a useful new comment.
before: Ticket T-42 is created by event E1. E1 arrives again. A fresh event E2 says the expected total is six.
try: Write down the ticket ID, the event IDs and the session ID. Decide whether each event starts a job or updates an existing one.
after: E1 starts one session. Its repeat starts none. E2 sends the new expected total to the same session.
why: A repeated delivery and a new piece of information should lead to different actions.
rescue: If you find two sessions, check when the creation event was first recorded. Look for an existing session before you start another paid job.

premise: A person can see a practice project. A scheduled helper cannot open the same file.
before: The person has a project grant through a team. The scheduled job signs in with a service account.
try: Write the two accounts on separate lines. For each line, check its team, assigned role and project grant. Try reading an allowed sample file under the intended test identity.
after: The check shows which account has a grant. A successful read by the person does not prove the service account has access.
why: Two workers can stand in front of the same door and carry different keys.
rescue: If the fix being considered gives every team more access, point to the one missing grant on the test sheet and ask its owner to review that one.

premise: A tool installed yesterday when the snapshot was made. A later session cannot fetch the same package.
before: The setup log says “installed.” Today’s practice run says it cannot reach the package site.
try: Write down where each command ran, its time, its package version and the first useful error. Ask the project owner to check which network rule applies to that worker and phase.
after: You have two distinct tests: the earlier snapshot build and the current running session. Each has a named machine and result.
why: The two phases can use different network rules. Looking at one computer’s success can send the search to the wrong place.
rescue: If the error actually says access denied, switch from checking the route to checking whether the right practice account may read that package.

premise: A session may have started even though your app never received an answer to its first request.
before: Ticket T-7 has a saved job record. Its create call was sent. The connection closed before a session ID came back.
try: Mark that record unknown. Use a permitted reader to look for the matching tag, time and account. Test what your app does when the same ticket arrives again.
after: A clear match attaches the existing session to T-7. A second delivery finds the same record. An unclear match waits for review.
why: Sending another create call straight away could start a second job for the same ticket.
rescue: If matching by tag finds two candidates, compare the job details and ask the owner. A tag alone is not a unique receipt.

premise: Twelve reports share a new date rule. One bad example could give all twelve the same wrong result.
before: Use two sample inputs: a real date and an empty field. The owner says a missing date stays empty.
try: Test one report built with the shared date tool and one that formats its own dates. Open both exported files in the app that reads them.
after: Each file shows the chosen date style. Neither file turns the blank into a date.
why: Trying two different kinds of reports can reveal a problem that twelve identical tests would miss.
rescue: If either file invents a date, pause the next group. Fix the shared example, then rerun the check on every open change.

premise: A team wants a fair number for its weekly cost per accepted change.
before: Ten sample jobs used 72 ACUs. Six changes passed review. Two are still open and two closed without a fix.
try: Divide the whole week’s units by the six accepted changes. Mark the date on the result. Keep reviewer minutes in a separate column.
after: The current cost is 12 units per accepted change. A money estimate also needs the team’s own price per unit.
why: An open request is still waiting. Counting it as a finished change makes the result look better than it is.
rescue: If the number came from dividing 72 by ten, label that as units per assigned job. Use six for the accepted-change question.

premise: You are reviewing a change that claims it fixed a fee report and ran every check.
before: The input has A for 350 cents, B for 200 cents and a repeat of A for 350 cents. The full export test stopped before opening its database.
try: Calculate the fee yourself. Then divide the claimed checks into ones that finished and ones that stopped. Ask for the actual exported file once its test can run.
after: The correct total is $5.50. A small test can pass while the full export remains unverified.
why: A right number in one check and a completed test of the whole export answer two different questions.
rescue: If the review says everything passed, request the first startup error and a fresh run that reaches the file. Open that file and read the total.

premise: A short game rule has one catch. Try an effort setting that can find it quickly.
before: Keep red cards unless they have a star. Your hand is red dot, red star, blue dot and red moon.
try: Ask for the cards to keep. If an answer misses the exception, use a higher effort with the same hand in a fresh chat.
after: Keep red dot and red moon. Circle each saved card on paper and check that neither has a star.
why: Repeating the same hand shows whether the setting helped. Changing the rule at the same time would hide the reason.
rescue: If the blue dot slips in, ask for each card’s color and shape in separate boxes, then apply the rule to both boxes.

premise: Two helpers label short notes for a sample app. A fast answer is valuable only when its label is right.
before: A toy run costs 6 cents and labels 3 notes correctly. Another costs 8 cents and labels 8 correctly.
try: Divide each bill by its number of correct labels. Keep the pretend totals separate from the live prices in the chapter.
after: The first run costs 2 cents per correct label. The second costs 1 cent per correct label.
why: A higher bill for the batch can still buy more usable answers per cent.
rescue: If you divided by all the notes, cross out the labels you cannot use. Divide by the accepted count and show the units.

premise: Two boxes of game pieces have very different sizes. A chart should show how many pieces people used altogether.
before: Box A has 90 of 100 pieces in use. Box B has 1 of 10 in use.
try: Ask for the total used and total available before the percentage. Add each pair by hand.
after: 91 of 110 pieces are in use. That is about 82.7%.
why: Each piece has one vote in this question. The large box holds ten times as many pieces as the small box.
rescue: If the answer says 50%, it most likely averaged the two box percentages. Ask it to divide 91 by 110.

premise: The player marks a word, turns a page and expects the mark to stay put.
before: Make three sample puzzle pages. On page two the word to find is LANTERN.
try: Ask Codex for top page buttons. On page two, mark LANTERN, tap Next, then Previous. On the last page, also try Next.
after: Back on page two, LANTERN still has its mark. The last page stays inside the book.
why: The button must preserve the game state as well as change the page number.
rescue: If the highlight vanishes, tell Codex the six exact actions you took and ask for a test that performs the same trip.

premise: Coach Alex needs a nameplate that someone across a table can read.
before: The design calls for one whistle above the words Coach Alex. The drawing should leave a wide blank band for the name.
try: Generate the picture without lettering. Add the title as editable words in your layout app. Zoom out to the physical size you intend to print.
after: Both words are clear, the spelling is right and the whistle is still easy to recognize.
why: Keeping the title editable lets you fix a letter without making a new picture.
rescue: If the whistle covers the name, ask for a smaller whistle near the top. Keep the existing text and check the layout again.

premise: A shift notice gives a change date but never names the person in charge.
before: Approved note: “Early shift starts at 8 on May 6.” Draft note: “Early shift starts May 5.”
try: Give Copilot only the approved note first. Ask for date, time and owner. Add the draft and ask it to list the difference on two lines.
after: The approved answer gives May 6 at 8 and says owner unknown. The comparison shows May 5 only in the draft.
why: A source can settle one field and leave another blank. A second source can also introduce a conflict.
rescue: If the helper adds an owner, request the exact line that names one. Remove that name from your report when the line is missing.

premise: Your reminder must distinguish a request for a new time from a confirmed change.
before: A practice Outlook thread says “Tuesday works.” Then: “Could we move to Wednesday?” The reply is “I will check.”
try: Ask Copilot for the last confirmed day and the open question. Follow any message link in its answer. Write a one-line draft reply.
after: Tuesday is the last confirmed day. Wednesday is still a request. A good reply asks whether Wednesday now works.
why: The newest message can leave a question open without replacing the earlier decision.
rescue: If the reminder says Wednesday is settled, ask it to quote a firm promise. Remove the claim if no message gives one.

premise: You are making a four-slide summary of a trial. A chart headline could change the meaning of the vote.
before: 12 teams were invited. Nine answered. Six of the nine said yes.
try: In Word, write one sentence for each count. Give the checked note to PowerPoint and ask for four slides. Read the slide titles without looking at the chart.
after: A valid title says “Six of nine replies favor continuing.” Another valid statement says half of all invited teams gave a yes.
why: Six is two thirds of nine but only one half of twelve. The group being counted belongs in the label.
rescue: If the title says most invited teams favor continuing, replace invited teams with respondents or show the 6-of-12 number explicitly.

premise: A formula should update after one batch changes. A number typed by hand may still show the old result.
before: The four batches have packed counts 120, 60, 20 and 0. Their rejected counts are 6, 6, 8 and 0.
try: Add Accepted as Packed minus Rejected. Find the total accepted, then change the second rejected count from 6 to 9.
after: The first total is 180. The new total is 177. Out of 200 packed, 177 accepted gives 88.5%.
why: The three extra rejects cut the accepted count by three. A check with a changed cell tests whether the formula stays connected.
rescue: If the total stays at 180, click the result cell and look for a formula. Check that its range includes the second batch.

premise: A game exporter splits a room label into two columns because the label contains a comma.
before: The sample room label is “Deck A, Row 2.” Your table has one Room column.
try: Ask GitHub Copilot to make a test that exports the label and reads it back. Then inspect the reopened table, not just the line of text in the file.
after: The new table still has one Room column. Its cell still reads Deck A, Row 2 with the comma in the middle.
why: CSV files use commas between columns. They need a way to keep a comma inside a piece of text.
rescue: If two columns appear, ask for correct CSV quoting and run the same round-trip test. Also try a plain label with no comma.

premise: You ask a personal helper for a checklist you could use at game night.
before: Your entire source says “Cards, pencil, setup at six.” It gives no address, guests or ticket price.
try: Ask Muse for a draft checklist from those words alone. Open the finished file in Library if one was made. On paper, mark each item that came from the source.
after: The list has cards, a pencil and setup at six. It can leave other details open.
why: A finished-looking file might add a plausible time or cost. Checking three small facts takes less time than fixing a bad invite later.
rescue: If the file adds a guest or address, ask it to remove that detail. Reopen the file instead of assuming the chat message changed it.

premise: Make your first packing list. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: A note reads: hat, pencil, hat, cup.
try: Count the lines. Put a tick beside each item in the note as you read the answer.
after: Three lines in order: hat, pencil, cup.
why: You can check a small sample by hand before trusting a longer answer.
rescue: If hat appears twice, ask for each different item just once.

premise: Pick a thinking level for a tiny puzzle. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Blue goes after Red. Gold goes before Red. There are three turns.
try: Try the same request in a fresh chat at another available level. Check both lists with three paper slips.
after: Gold, Red, Blue satisfies both rules. Only passing answers count.
why: More thinking time can help, but the rules and your test decide whether the answer works.
rescue: If Blue comes first, underline the word after. Ask the tool to test that rule against its own list.

premise: Give directions by voice. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Draw three circles on paper. Mark the left one A and the right one C. Leave the middle one empty.
try: Listen to the letters it repeats. Change your question to ask which circle holds C.
after: B belongs in the middle. C is on the right.
why: Speaking and listening can change a word. Repeat the important detail and check it.
rescue: If it heard D, say the letters one by one. You can type the same words in Chat.

premise: Make a helper that gives one hint. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Practice riddle: I have keys but no locks. The intended answer is a piano.
try: Ask for a hint, then type Reveal. Check the two replies separately.
after: The hint leaves piano out. The second reply says piano and links the keys to music.
why: A saved rule should work again in a new chat. Change the sample to find out.
rescue: If the first reply spoils it, edit the instructions and start a fresh test conversation with the Gem.

premise: Build a playable tap counter. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Make a new page with a score of zero, a button called Score, and a Reset button.
try: Open Preview. Tap Score twice, then once more. Try Reset.
after: Scores run 0, 1, 2, 3. The win appears only at 3. Reset gives 0.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If Reset leaves the win message behind, ask to clear the message and score together. Play again.

premise: Open your first source citation. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Add a source called Schedule with the text: Practice starts at 2. Bring a pencil.
try: Tap the little source mark beside the answer. Find the time in the note itself.
after: The answer is 2. The line about the pencil supplies no time.
why: A source mark is a starting point. The line it opens must actually support the answer.
rescue: If it says 2 p.m., look for p.m. in the note. Ask for the exact wording since the note leaves that part open.

premise: Hand off a packing job and check the result. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Kit list: 2 red flags, 1 blue flag, 3 cones. You want a list to pack.
try: Open the task thread. Count the lines and add the quantities by hand.
after: Three lines list red flags 2, blue flag 1 and cones 3. Total items packed would be 6.
why: A finished message is a claim. Read the result and compare it with the starting note.
rescue: If it makes six lines, ask for one line for each kind of item, with its count beside it.

premise: Edit a research plan before the search. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Question: How do I make flashcards in Gemini Notebook on an iPad?
try: Read the plan first. Remove any task about prices. Start the search and open its cited Google guide.
after: The brief answers the three actions with support from the mobile guide. Pricing is outside this job.
why: Two pages can use the same words for different tools. Read the part that matches the job.
rescue: If it cites a general web tutorial, ask it to find the official iPad instructions and point to the flashcard section.

premise: Use two sources without mixing them up. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Add note Rules: A star earns 2 points. Add note Round: The blue team drew 3 stars.
try: Open both citations. Multiply the score for one star by the number drawn.
after: Rules gives 2. Round gives 3. Blue earned 6 points.
why: A source mark is a starting point. The line it opens must actually support the answer.
rescue: If only one note is cited, ask where the other number came from. Check that both notes are selected.

premise: Two game cards agree on how to earn points and disagree on when to stop.
before: Old says one point per turn and a target of 8 on May 1. New keeps one point per turn and changes the target to 12 on May 4.
try: Build a Mind Map and open it in Studio. Expand a branch on scoring and pick a point. Ask Chat what changed, then open both dated sources.
after: Both notes share the points rule. The newer target is 12. With Old selected alone, the only target you can prove is 8.
why: A branch connects ideas. The date and the words in New tell you which rule to use.
rescue: If the map shows only “scoring,” select that point and ask Chat for both dates. Read Old and New side by side before choosing a winner.

premise: Make a word guessing game. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Secret word LAMP. The player types a guess. A blank guess should never count.
try: Try a blank, then desk, then space-lamp-space. Click Guess once after the win.
after: Blank leaves 0. Desk gives 1. The last word wins in 2. Extra clicks leave 2.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If typing lamp fails, ask the app to trim the spaces and compare both words in the same case.

premise: Teach a helper to read a mailbox list. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Pretend rows: Box A, shared. Box B, room. Box C, shared.
try: Test the Gem with the three rows. Then remove the type from Box C and run it again.
after: First result: 2, A and C. Second: 1 shared, A. C is unknown.
why: A saved rule should work again in a new chat. Change the sample to find out.
rescue: If a blank becomes shared, add a rule to the Gem that a missing type cannot be guessed.

premise: Make a three-card study deck. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Add one note: A folder holds files. A prompt is a request. A source is material used to answer.
try: Open the flashcards in Studio. Say a meaning aloud before flipping each card. Mark one card missed and review it again.
after: Each of the three words has a meaning supported by the note. You can explain your missed one after review.
why: A source mark is a starting point. The line it opens must actually support the answer.
rescue: If a card asks about a new word, compare it to the note. Request a deck limited to the three listed words.

premise: Practice reading a result before scoring a tool. This made-up example could come from any builder.
before: The first game opens at Blue 0, Gold 0. Blue gets Question 1 right. The first tap shows Blue 2, Gold 0.
try: Tap the same choice again straight away. Look at both totals, the question number and the active team. Finish the game and check the other four rules on the page.
after: Suppose the second tap changes Blue to 4. Mark the click-lock check Fail and record both scores. If all four other checks pass, the first-try score is 4 out of 5.
why: Two taps on one answer count as just one pick. The number on the screen lets another reader repeat your check.
rescue: If the screen changes too fast to tell, restart and repeat the double tap. Leave the check untested until you can tell what happened. Keep this first file when you try the later edit.

premise: Capstone: Build a quiz from a checked rulebook. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Score note: red earns 3, blue earns 2. Turn note: two rounds, one card per round.
try: Check the evidence in Notebook. Use Canvas to build a quiz from your three verified questions. Ask for a score and Play again. Answer all three correctly, then miss one on a new game.
after: Each answer traces to a note. Two red cards earn 6. The first game scores 3 of 3. Missing one in the second scores 2 of 3.
why: A source mark is a starting point. The line it opens must actually support the answer.
rescue: If the quiz adds a prize for winning, point to the notes. Remove that extra rule from the game and test again.

premise: Turn mixed notes into a neat table. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Three notes: Red has 4. Green has 0. Blue has no score yet.
try: Read each row and circle only the teams that have played, including the team with zero.
after: Red 4, Green 0, Blue dash. Two scores are known.
why: You can check a small sample by hand before trusting a longer answer.
rescue: If Blue gets zero, ask which line says Blue has played. Put back the dash.

premise: Play a mystery-object game by voice. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Use a pretend object: a cup. Its clues are hollow, holds water, sits on a table.
try: After the first clue say Next clue. Then say Reveal. Check the written conversation if you missed a word.
after: One clue comes first. The second turn adds one more. The reveal names the cup.
why: Speaking and listening can change a word. Repeat the important detail and check it.
rescue: If all clues arrive together, interrupt with a request for one clue per turn. Use typed Chat if Live is unavailable.

premise: Create a three-line release note helper. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: A score button used to add two points. It now adds one. The test used three taps.
try: Give the Gem the example. Then request a note for an update that has no test result yet.
after: The first note says three taps now give 3. A missing test is listed as unknown.
why: A saved rule should work again in a new chat. Change the sample to find out.
rescue: If it claims all tests passed, edit the Gem to ask for the missing check. Start with a fresh change.

premise: Review a task before it shares anything. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Draft event: game night, 6 p.m., Room A. No guest list is provided.
try: Inspect the task’s plan and output. Read the guest line. Finish with the draft on screen.
after: The draft has a title, time and room. It has no made-up guests and nothing was sent.
why: A finished message is a claim. Read the result and compare it with the starting note.
rescue: If a send action is proposed, leave it unapproved and ask for plain text in the task thread.

premise: Build a glossary from one source. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Add a note: deck means a stack of cards; draw means take the top card; discard means put a card aside.
try: Open the source for each meaning. Mark which words were in the note and which lines are invented examples.
after: All three definitions match the note. The examples are clearly marked as practice.
why: A source mark is a starting point. The line it opens must actually support the answer.
rescue: If draw becomes making a picture, select only the card note and ask what draw means in this game.

premise: Make a two-choice story. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Start in a cave with two doors. Blue leads to a lake. Gold leads to a library.
try: Choose Blue and go back. Choose Gold and go back. Count all the available endings.
after: Blue always reaches the lake. Gold always reaches the library. Both return to the start.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If both doors open the same ending, ask for separate click actions. Try each path from the start.

premise: Check a schedule with two rules. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: There are three time slots: 1, 2, 3. Setup must come before Play. Cleanup must be last.
try: Write the slots on paper. Try the proposed swap yourself. If your account offers thinking levels, compare Low and High in separate chats.
after: Setup, Play, Cleanup works. Swapping the first two breaks the first rule.
why: More thinking time can help, but the rules and your test decide whether the answer works.
rescue: If the answer just says it works, ask it to point to the numbers for Setup and Play after the swap.

premise: Build a two-source fact sheet. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Compare two official Google topics: turning on Gemini Live and making a Notebook flashcard.
try: Before starting, check that the plan asks for both distinct products. Open each final link and look for its action.
after: The Live row points to Live controls. The flashcard row points to Notebook Studio. Neither row borrows the other app’s menus.
why: Two pages can use the same words for different tools. Read the part that matches the job.
rescue: If the links just open the same homepage, ask for the specific help articles and inspect their headings.

premise: A study-night guide needs one tip about flashcards and one checked ticket price.
before: Packing says badge. Times says 4. Rumor guesses 9 coins. Search the web inside the notebook for how to study missed flashcards.
try: Try Fast Research, then Deep Research. Inspect each imported web page. Keep the help page that explains missed cards. Clear Rumor and any unverified page before asking the study-night question.
after: The help page supports another round of missed cards. The checked event notes give badge and 4. The price is unknown until Fare supplies 2 game coins.
why: A useful search result can answer the flashcard question. It cannot set a price for a made-up event.
rescue: If the answer says 9, ask it to point to that number in a selected source. Clear Rumor and the research report, then ask a fresh question.

premise: Build a live wait-list tool. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: A pretend queue starts empty. Visitors take tickets A, B and C in order.
try: Add A, B and C. Serve twice. Add D. Clear. Try to serve once more.
after: A and then B are served. C and D wait in order. Clear leaves an empty list with no ticket to serve.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If D is served before C, ask it to remove only the oldest waiting ticket. Replay from empty.

premise: Turn a task result into a usable run sheet. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Practice event: setup 3 minutes, game 7 minutes, cleanup 2 minutes. Start at minute 0.
try: Open the finished file or table. Change game time to 5 in a follow-up task. Compare the start of cleanup in both versions.
after: First cleanup starts at minute 10 and ends at 12. The changed version starts at 8 and ends at 10.
why: A finished message is a claim. Read the result and compare it with the starting note.
rescue: If the last end time stays 12, ask it to compute every time again from the changed duration.

premise: Two audio hosts explain mailbox types. You need to pick the one that stands for a meeting space.
before: Team says a shared box serves a team. Room says a room box represents a meeting space.
try: Generate a new English Deep Dive. In Interactive Mode, choose Join while it plays. Ask which box fits a meeting space. When the hosts answer, open the Room note and check the words.
after: A room mailbox fits a meeting space. A shared box serves a team. Each part traces to its own note.
why: Spoken answers go by quickly. Writing down a claim gives you something to match to the source.
rescue: If the hosts invent a booking fee, open both notes and look for a price. Mark the fee unknown. If Join is hidden, reopen the new English audio in your notebook.

premise: Build a read-only mailbox tally. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Paste these pretend rows: A,shared; B,room; C,shared; D,unknown.
try: Press Count. Change C to room and press Count again. Inspect the original pasted text after each run.
after: First: shared 2, room 1, unknown 1. Next: shared 1, room 2, unknown 1. The input stays as typed.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If unknown disappears, add an Unknown group. Add another unknown row and watch only that group grow.

premise: Capstone: Ship a two-player score keeper. Work through this small example before trying your own.
before: Each team starts at 0. Any turn may give +5 or −5. The first team at 10 wins.
try: Give Blue +5, Red −5, Blue +5. Try a score after the win. Undo, then start a new game.
after: Blue wins 10 to −5. Extra taps do nothing. Undo restores Blue 5 and play resumes. New game sets both to 0.
why: A button can look right and still do the wrong thing. Trying the full path checks what a player will see.
rescue: If undo changes Red instead, keep a list of moves in order. Undo only the last recorded move, then retest.

premise: A tiny help desk needs four answers it can prove or label unknown.
before: Rows lists A shared, B room and C shared. Types explains the boxes. Limit says read only. The notes give no price.
try: Make a Data Table and a Slide Deck in Studio. Check the table row for shared boxes and count the shared boxes pictured on the slides. Copy the checked lines into a Canvas app and press each button.
after: A is shared. A and C make two shared boxes. Limit rules out edits. Cost stays unknown across the app and any Studio output that mentions cost.
why: A tidy table or slide can still contain a mistake. Checking each output against the original rows keeps one wrong total out of the app.
rescue: If a slide counts three shared boxes, read Rows aloud. Generate a corrected slide. Keep the verified count of two in the app and retest all four buttons.

premise: Two players race to light ten lanterns. Test the finish line and play a second round.
before: Start both players on 0. Moves are +1 or +2. The goal is 10.
try: Choose +2 for both players in turn. Keep going until the first player reaches ten. Try another move after the win. Choose New race. Choose +1 for the first move. Read both scores and whose turn comes next.
after: The first player wins on move nine with scores 10 and 8. Another move cannot raise either score. The new scores are 1 and 0. It is the second player's turn. The old winner message has cleared.
why: Taking turns needs two pieces of memory: each player's score and which player moves next.
rescue: If a move after the win still counts, have the game check for a winner before accepting a move.

premise: Flip pairs on a small memory board. Catch a mismatch and prove a matched pair stays open.
before: Use four fixed positions: Moon, Bell, Bell, Moon. All cards start face down.
try: Flip positions one and two. Read the words. Select Turn back. Then flip one and four. Click a Moon again. Match positions two and three. Start a new board.
after: The first pair closes again. Both Moon cards stay open after the match. One pair has been found. The repeat click adds nothing. Both matches win the game. New board hides all four cards and sets pairs to zero.
why: Cards have a face, a place and a saved match state. The game should remember all three.
rescue: If double-clicking one card makes a match, ask for two different card positions before checking the words.

premise: Check off the items for a pretend walk. A counter lets you see what still belongs in your bag.
before: Items in order: hat, bottle, map. All start unchecked.
try: Check hat and map. Look at the counter, uncheck hat and read it again. Check the other two items. Select Clear checks after the Ready message appears.
after: The count moves from 2 of 3 to 1 of 3. Only map stays checked. The count reaches 3 of 3, then returns to 0 of 3. All three item labels remain on the list.
why: Checking a box sets its state. Rebuilding the total from the checked boxes avoids counting taps that undo earlier taps.
rescue: If unchecking raises the number, ask for a count of the boxes currently checked after every click.

premise: Make bars you can compare by eye. Keep the printed numbers so the shortest bar still makes sense.
before: Use practice folders Inbox=6, Drafts=2, Archive=0.
try: Read all three labels. Compare the lengths of the first two bars. Look at Archive. Change Drafts to 4. Then clear that field. Fill it with 0 and read the total.
after: The total is 8. Inbox is three times as long as Drafts. Archive shows 0 next to its label. The totals are 10, then a request for the missing count, then 6. The empty box never pretends to be a real zero.
why: A picture helps people spot a large folder. The written number tells them exactly how large it is.
rescue: If zero removes the whole Archive row, keep the text label and number even when the bar has no length.

premise: Use two buttons to move through a short route. A reader should always know where they are.
before: Stops are Dock, Bridge, Gate in that order.
try: Start the page. Try Previous. Press Next twice. Read the last stop and try Next again. Press Previous once, then First stop. Check the selected stop both times.
after: Dock says 1 of 3 with Previous off. Gate says 3 of 3 with Next off. Bridge is 2 of 3. First stop returns to Dock, with Previous off again.
why: The button changes a position in a list. Its label and the printed count should both follow that same position.
rescue: If you reach a blank stop, have the code check the first and last positions before moving.

premise: Let a reader make a sample sentence bigger without letting it grow off the screen.
before: Start at 18 pixels. The allowed sizes are 14, 16, 18, 20, 22 and 24.
try: Press Larger three times, then try it once more. Compare the printed number and the actual sentence. Press Reset. Press Smaller until it stops. Reset once more.
after: The size stops at 24. A fourth press does not grow the sentence. Reset gives 18 each time. Smaller stops at 14. Everything fits in a narrow browser window.
why: The printed size gives you a second way to judge what changed when the letters grew.
rescue: If the number changes but the sentence does not, ask the page to set the sample text size from that same number.

premise: Walk from tile to tile to spell a word. A jump across the board should never count.
before: Use a two-row grid. Top row C A T. Bottom row R P N. The target is CAT.
try: Click C then T. Watch whether T enters the trail. Now add A and T in order. Start over. Try C,A,C. Then clear the trail and make the winning path again.
after: The jump from C to T is refused. C, A, T spells CAT and wins. The used C cannot be added twice. Clear removes the selection. A new correct path still wins.
why: Two tiles can be close on paper without sharing a side. A game needs a rule for exactly which neighbors count.
rescue: If a diagonal tile works, check row and column changes. One should move by one while the other stays the same.

premise: Turn on two filters and check that only the matching rows stay on the page.
before: A: unread, flagged. B: read, flagged. C: unread, plain. D: read, plain.
try: Select Unread only. Now select Flagged only too. Read which IDs are still on the page. Turn off Unread only while keeping Flagged only on. Then select Reset filters.
after: Unread shows A and C. Both boxes show just A, with count 1. Flagged alone shows A and B. Reset shows A, B, C and D, with count 4.
why: Two filters together work like two gates. Each row must pass each gate that you have closed.
rescue: If C appears with both boxes checked, test the two flags on the same row before showing it.

premise: Share a small bill without losing a penny when division gives a remainder.
before: Try 10.00 dollars for 3 people. Use seats 1, 2 and 3.
try: Enter 10.00 and 3, then press Split. Add the three printed shares yourself. Try 0.02 for 3 seats and then 0.00 for 2 seats. Finally try zero seats.
after: Seats 1, 2 and 3 owe 3.34, 3.33 and 3.33. Their sum is 10.00. The shares are 0.01, 0.01, 0.00. Both zero-dollar shares are 0.00. Zero seats gives a helpful error.
why: A whole cent cannot be sliced into thirds. Giving the first seats the spare pennies keeps the total exact.
rescue: If all three seats owe 3.33 for 10.00, count the pennies left over after the equal shares.

premise: Put colored blocks on a day's time line. Let a meeting begin the minute the earlier meeting ends.
before: Room A has a booking from 09:00 to 09:30. New requests use whole minutes on this same day.
try: Ask for 09:15–09:45. Then try 09:30–10:00. Count the blocks after each request. Try 10:00–10:00 and 10:15–10:00. Restore the sample and try 08:30–09:00.
after: The first request overlaps, so the count stays one. The second fits and makes two blocks. Both bad lengths are refused. After reset the earlier meeting fits beside the original one.
why: Imagine sliding two books together on a shelf. Their covers may touch even though their pages never overlap.
rescue: If touching events clash, check whether there is at least one minute inside both bookings.

premise: Enter a score for either team. Take back the last turn without losing earlier turns.
before: Start Red and Blue at 0. Enter Red +7, Blue +4, then Red -2.
try: Enter the three sample turns in order. Undo the last one, then undo the one before it. Enter Blue -3 after the undos. Select New game. Try Undo again.
after: The first totals are Red 5 and Blue 4. Undo gives 7 and 4, then 7 and 0. Blue shows -3 before reset. New game shows two zeros and no turns. Undo is off.
why: Store the turns as slips in a stack. Undo takes only the top slip from the stack.
rescue: If Undo removes points from the wrong team, save a team label with each turn instead of reading the currently selected team.

premise: Assign seat cards in order. Show exactly which card goes on the waiting list when the table fills up.
before: The table has two seats. The first three card IDs are A1, B2 and C3.
try: Add A1, B2, C3, then C3 again. Look at both seats and the waiting list. Release A1. Add D4. Then release B2. Read the seat labels and waiting list.
after: A1 and B2 are seated. C3 appears once on the waiting list. C3 takes the first seat. D4 waits, then takes the second seat. The waiting list ends empty.
why: A waiting list works like a line at a door. A new arrival must get behind people already there.
rescue: If D4 jumps ahead, take from the front of the waiting list whenever a seat opens.

premise: Use a table preview to catch rows that would disappear or change when you save a report.
before: Rows are Queue=5, Archive=0, and Review with an empty count. The heading is folder,count.
try: Preview the three rows. Download the file and open it with a text editor. Check the comma at the end of the last row. Use the file picker to read the saved CSV into the page. Count rows and inspect both the zero and the empty cell.
after: The data lines are Queue,5 then Archive,0 then Review, with nothing after its comma. The restored preview has three rows. Archive is still 0. Review still has an empty count.
why: The return trip proves the saved file holds the same facts the preview showed. Looking at the preview alone cannot prove that.
rescue: If Review comes back with 0, test for an empty cell before turning its contents into a number.

premise: Run two full memory rounds and compare the scores. Both players should get the same board and rules.
before: Each player gets four fixed cards in order Sun, Key, Key, Sun. One revealed pair counts as one try.
try: For player one, choose 1+2 (miss), 1+4 (match), 2+3 (match). Advance to player two. Choose 1+4 and 2+3. Start again. Have each player match both pairs in two tries. Look for the result, and check the reset board once more.
after: The first player used three tries. The second used two. The second player wins. The second tournament ends in a tie at two tries each. No card stays open from the previous tournament.
why: A useful finish screen shows the numbers that caused the result. You can check both the game and its winner.
rescue: If the second player inherits open cards, reset the board between players while keeping the completed first score.

premise: Build the whole path from a local file to a checked report. A reviewer should be able to see why a row needs attention.
before: CSV heading box,used,limit. Rows: A,90,100 then B,0,100 then C,,100 then D,5,0.
try: Load the four rows. Inspect the labels, totals and four checks. Download the report and inspect all rows in a text editor. Change A to 89 and fill C with 50. Run on the changed input. Finally press Load sample and rerun the built-in checks.
after: A is Warning, B is OK, C and D are Review. Counts are 1 Warning, 1 OK, 2 Review. The file contains four rows. The changed counts are 0 Warning, 3 OK, 1 Review. Reloading the sample restores the original counts and four passing checks.
why: The input, preview, downloaded file and independent checks tell the same story in different ways. That gives a reviewer something solid to verify.
rescue: If B or D is missing, keep a row for every input. Test for a bad limit before dividing, and test a real zero separately from an empty value.

premise: Guess whether the next card is higher or lower. A fixed deck lets you check the score by hand.
before: Deck in order: 4, 7, 3, 9. Show the 4 first.
try: Guess Higher, Lower, Higher. Note the card and score after each press. Play again and choose Lower first. Finish the other two guesses correctly.
after: The revealed cards are 7, 3, 9. The score reaches 3 out of 3. Guesses stop. The first new guess earns 0. The second game ends at 2 out of 3.
why: A fixed deck makes the answer key easy to check. Once the game works, you could offer a shuffled deck for play.
rescue: If you can score twice from one card, move to the next card after every guess and close the buttons at the end.

premise: A player earns a point each time two dice show the same number. Give the game a practice roll so you can prove the rule.
before: Practice rolls: 2 and 2, then 2 and 5, then 6 and 6.
try: Use Practice roll three times. Read the numbers each time and tally matches on paper. Try a fourth roll. Start again and use Roll for three turns. Inspect the values and the finish message.
after: The scores after each try are 1, 1 and 2. Two matching pairs win two points. The fourth roll cannot change the finished game. A new game starts at zero. Each random die stays between 1 and 6.
why: An example you can repeat tests the rules. Random rolls make the same game worth playing again.
rescue: If a seven appears, ask the code for whole values from one through six and test the end points using a fixed pair.

premise: Move a timer forward by hand. A reader can learn the controls without waiting five real minutes.
before: Set the practice timer to 5 minutes. One Tick removes 1 minute.
try: Press Tick before Start. Then Start and press Tick twice. Read the number and press Pause. Tick while paused. Resume with Start and tick until zero. Try one more tick, then Reset.
after: Before Start the timer stays at 5. After the two ticks it reads 3. The paused tick makes no change. After three more counted ticks the timer stops at 0. Reset returns to 5.
why: A pretend clock lets you check pause and finish instantly. The same rules can later be wired to a real clock.
rescue: If Pause still spends a minute, have Tick check whether the timer is running before changing the count.

premise: Build two buttons for a stack of pretend tickets. Stop the count from falling below zero.
before: Begin with 2 open tickets. Each New ticket adds one. Each Close one removes one.
try: Click Close one twice. Read the count and try to close another ticket. Click New ticket twice, then Close one. Restore the sample.
after: The count ends at 0 with All clear. A third close cannot make -1. The count reaches 1 before reset. Restore sample brings back 2 open tickets.
why: A count is the state of the tool. Each button needs a rule for changing it and a rule for when to stop.
rescue: If the last action says Closed for a blocked click, update both the count and that message only after an allowed action.

premise: A three-question quiz can give helpful feedback even when every answer is wrong.
before: Questions and keys: two plus three=5, seven minus four=3, twice four=8. Include one wrong choice per question.
try: Choose the right answer on all three. On each question try to press the answer twice before going on. Replay once with all wrong answers. Replay again with only the middle answer correct.
after: Only the first selection counts. The final screen says Perfect and 3 out of 3. The two screens say Review at 0 out of 3 and Keep practicing at 1 out of 3.
why: The end message depends on the final count. Trying the two ends and a middle score checks all three messages.
rescue: If all scores say Perfect, inspect the rule for each possible count and run the three routes again.

premise: Use a choice to show the right card. Two readers can choose different moods without typing a prompt.
before: Choices: Calm gives Draw a cloud. Curious gives Find a pattern. Bold gives Try a puzzle.
try: Choose Curious and then Bold. Read each card and count how many cards are showing. Clear the choice. Pick Calm twice. Count the cards and read the instruction.
after: Curious shows Find a pattern. Bold replaces it with Try a puzzle. Only one card is on screen. Clear hides all activity cards. Choosing Calm twice still shows just one Draw a cloud card.
why: The selected mood is like an index tab. Re-selecting it should reveal the same page once.
rescue: If old cards pile up, ask the app to replace the displayed card whenever the choice changes.

premise: A mystery card can reveal one hint at a time. Solve it early to keep more points.
before: Target word is LANTERN. Hints in order: You carry me. I hold a light. I can hang from a hook.
try: Give two hints. Type lantern with a space at each end. Check the guess. Replay. Try lamp, then use every hint and finish with LANTERN.
after: Two different hints appear. The round ends with 2 points. More hints or checks cannot add points. Lamp keeps the game going. The last correct guess earns 1 point. The three hints appear in order.
why: A hint is a trade: it makes a guess easier in exchange for a point. The same hint must never cost twice.
rescue: If a guess with spaces fails, trim the outer spaces and compare both words in the same case.

premise: Plan three meals and add up the ingredients. Use a second serving to test whether the list really changes.
before: Meal cards: Soup needs 2 carrots and 1 onion. Wrap needs 1 carrot and 2 beans. Days are One, Two and Three.
try: Choose Soup, Wrap, Soup on the three days. Check the shopping list. Clear Day Three, then switch Day Two from Wrap to Soup. Read the new totals and clear the whole board.
after: You need 5 carrots, 2 onions and 2 beans. After both changes the list has 4 carrots, 2 onions and no beans. Clear gives an empty list.
why: Adding the whole board again after an edit prevents the old meal from hiding in the shopping list.
rescue: If beans remain after both wraps are gone, rebuild the totals from the current three choices.

premise: Pick out missing dates, impossible dates and real leap days. A colored label needs words as well as color.
try: Load the four rows. Compare the two February dates and sort them into groups on paper. Change R2 to 2027-02-28 and fill R3 with 2027-04-31. Count the groups again.
after: R1 and R4 are Valid. R2 says Check date. R3 says Missing. Counts are 2, 1 and 1. Three rows are Valid. One says Check date. None say Missing.
why: February can have an extra day in one year but not in the next. Matching a date-shaped pattern cannot prove a date is real.
rescue: If April 31 passes, compare the entered day with the number of days in that month. Test both February rows again.

premise: A reader types part of a word and gets matching dishes. Changing the input should refresh the same list.
before: Menu: Pear pie, Bean soup, Peach toast, Corn bowl.
try: Type PE with a space on either side. Count the dishes and check their order. Try bowl, then stone, then clear the box.
after: Pear pie and Peach toast appear in that order. Bean soup and Corn bowl are hidden. The results are Corn bowl, a no-match message, then all four dishes.
why: A search box is like a paper window over a list. It should reveal matching rows without tearing up the full list.
rescue: If clearing the box still leaves an empty menu, keep an untouched copy of the original list and search that on each change.

premise: Pick a seat on a simple map and hear or read its label. A blocked seat should never count as a booking.
before: The map has seats A1 A2 in the top row, B1 B2 in the bottom row. A2 starts blocked.
try: Choose B2 then A1. Try A2. Read the chosen list and use Confirm. Clear the selection, then use only Tab and Enter to choose B1. Confirm again.
after: The list says A1, B2. A2 stays Blocked. The confirmation lists the same two seats. After clearing, Confirm is off. The keyboard booking lists just B1.
why: Labels let a reader use the map even if colors look alike. Sorting seats by row keeps the summary easy to check.
rescue: If a keyboard press does nothing, use real buttons with text labels. Try moving and selecting again with the mouse set aside.

premise: A short list tells you which pieces of a fake notice are still missing before you export it.
before: Draft boxes: subject=Practice update, time=09:15, reply contact empty. Use help@example.test for the sample contact.
try: Load the draft. Fill the blank contact. Look at each status and the ready-to-copy notice. Set the time to 24:00. Fix it to 00:00. Then change the subject to spaces only.
after: At first only contact needs attention. Once filled, the notice includes Practice update, 09:15 and help@example.test. 24:00 fails and 00:00 passes. A subject made of spaces prevents a fresh ready notice.
why: A clear error beside one field saves readers from guessing why the whole form refused their notice.
rescue: If an old ready notice remains after a bad edit, hide or update it every time one input changes.

premise: A short code ties a group row to an owner row. Find out which rows have no match.
before: Group list: G1=Maps, G2=Charts, G3=Notes. Owner list: G2=Blue team, G1=Red team.
try: Rebuild the two lists. Check that the first group gets the second owner record. Add owner G9=Gold team. Add owner G3=Green team. Rebuild and look at both panels.
after: Maps gets Red team, Charts gets Blue team, Notes gets Unknown. There are zero unmatched owner IDs. Notes now gets Green team. G9 appears only in the unmatched box. There are still three group rows.
why: The ID is the matching sticker on two boxes. The order in which the boxes arrive does not decide which pair belongs together.
rescue: If Maps shows Blue team, match by G1 rather than pairing the first row with the first row.

premise: Build a short story a reader can win, lose and replay. The bag must remember a key between rooms.
before: Rooms: Lobby, Workshop, Gate. The Workshop has one brass key. The gate has a locked and unlocked ending.
try: Go straight to Gate and try to exit. Restart, visit Workshop, take the key twice, return to Lobby, then go to Gate and exit. Restart after the win. Inspect the bag and try the short losing route again.
after: The first route ends Locked out. The second ends Home free. The bag showed just one key. The new bag is empty and the losing route still works. A past win never unlocks a new game.
why: Rooms, items and endings are separate pieces of game memory. Test more than one route to prove they fit together.
rescue: If restart leaves the door open, reset the room, the bag and the ending together. Repeat both routes.

premise: A team has three pretend meeting slips. Build a usable board where every task points back to its exact source.
before: S1: Maps team will test on May 4. S2: Charts team will draw on May 5. S3: Notes team will review, date pending.
try: Load the sample. Approve S1 and S3. Export and read the two rows. Change S1's date to May 5. Run the check and try exporting again. Give the Charts task the wrong source ID S1. Run checks with that error, a made-up date on S3, and all three original cards.
after: The first export has the Maps test on May 4 and the Notes review with Pending. The changed card loses approval. Only the unchanged, approved S3 can export. Both wrong examples fail for named reasons. All three original cards pass. Restoring the sample resets approvals.
why: A date can be real and still belong to the wrong team. Tying the card to its own slip makes a wrong match easier to catch.
rescue: If any May 5 date passes on S1, compare the date with that one source. Scanning every slip for May 5 is too broad.

premise: Play against a pretend opponent. Its first three moves are fixed so you can check a win, a tie and a loss.
before: The computer plays Rock, Paper, Scissors in that order. Win earns 1, tie and loss earn 0.
try: Pick Paper for all three rounds. Read both moves each time and write down the result. Press Replay. Pick Paper, Scissors, Rock. Try one more press after round three.
after: The results are win, tie and loss in order. Final score is 1 of 3. The score resets before the game. Three wins give 3 of 3. The extra press cannot change the result.
why: A predictable opponent helps you test the rules. The player can still choose any move and finish a whole game.
rescue: If Paper loses to Rock, check the pair from the player's point of view. Test all three winning pairs.

premise: Find the item that does not belong with the others. Give the answer a reason as well as a point.
before: Round 1: spoon, fork, mitten (mitten is clothing). Round 2: bus, apple, tram (apple is fruit). Round 3: drum, flute, map (map is a guide).
try: Choose mitten, apple and drum. Try to change the last guess after the explanation appears. Replay and choose all three correct words. Read the last explanation before closing the game.
after: The first two are right. The third answer is map. Final score stays at 2 of 3. The second score is 3 of 3. Each round gives its own reason.
why: An explanation lets a player learn from a miss. The right answer should be set before you show the buttons.
rescue: If the last explanation mentions clothing, look up the reason on the current round's card.

premise: Let a reader save a palette. Reopening the same page should bring back the chosen colors.
before: Three starting color boxes: #112233, #445566, #778899. Use #ff9900 for the second-color test.
try: Change only the second color to #ff9900. Save and reload the same page in the same browser. Restore defaults. Save them and reload again.
after: The second code stays #ff9900. The first and third still match the starting values. All three original codes return and survive the reload. The message tells whether saving worked.
why: Saved choices belong to this browser and page. Another browser or private window can have a different storage box.
rescue: If the file page cannot save on your browser, have Claude give a local serving command. Open that address and repeat both reload tests.

premise: Give each practice ballot one vote. See how a tie looks before declaring a winner.
before: Choices are Soup, Wrap and Salad. Practice ballot IDs are T1, T2 and T3.
try: Vote T1 for Soup, T2 for Wrap, then try T1 for Salad. Read the totals. Give T3 to Wrap. Reset the poll and submit one ballot again.
after: Soup 1, Wrap 1, Salad 0. The highest counts tie. The repeated T1 is refused. Wrap leads with 2 before reset. All totals clear, and the new poll accepts the reused practice ID.
why: The ballot ID tracks who already voted while the vote count tracks the choice. They are different pieces of information.
rescue: If a repeated ID changes the poll, check the ID list before adding to a choice's total.

premise: Show how full a pretend mailbox is. Include a message for a missing size or an impossible limit.
before: Used 25, limit 100. Other test pairs are 0 and 100, 90 and 100, 5 and 0.
try: Try 25 and 100, then 0 and 100. Look at the printed percent and warning label. Try 90 and 100, then 5 and 0, then erase the used field. Read the message after each.
after: The pairs give 25 percent OK and 0 percent OK. Zero is a valid size. Ninety percent gives Warning. The zero limit and the empty used value both give Needs review.
why: A fraction needs something to divide by. Zero used is fine, but zero space allowed makes the fraction impossible.
rescue: If the screen shows Infinity, check the limit before dividing. If zero used disappears, check for a blank string first.

premise: Let a reader complete three steps before finishing a task. Undoing one check should reopen the task.
before: Steps: Read sample, Check total, Save note.
try: Check the first two steps. Try Finish. Then check the third and finish. Uncheck Check total. Inspect the status. Recheck it, finish, then press Start again.
after: Finish is off for two checks. With all three checked it marks the task Finished. Undoing a check clears Finished. Start again clears all boxes and disables Finish.
why: A finished stamp belongs to one particular set of checks. If that set changes, the stamp needs another review.
rescue: If two boxes enable Finish, count the current checked boxes against all three required steps.

premise: Move nearby number tiles into one empty space. Work a one-move puzzle and try a trick move.
before: Use a two-by-two board. Start [1,2,empty,3]. The goal is [1,2,3,empty].
try: At the start click tile 2 diagonally across from empty. Then click tile 3. Read the board and move count. Reset. Click tile 1, then tile 1 again to bring it back. Finish with tile 3.
after: The diagonal click changes nothing. Tile 3 slides left. The solved board shows one move. This route also solves the board. It takes three legal moves.
why: Two board pictures can look similar while the rules behind them differ. A diagonal test catches the wrong neighbor rule.
rescue: If tile 2 moves on the first click, compare the row and column distances. Their sum should be one.

premise: Compare two toy plans. Find the point where the cheaper plan changes as use grows.
before: Plan A costs 2 coins for each use. Plan B costs 5 coins plus 1 coin per use. Try 0, 4, 5 and 6 uses.
try: Set uses to 4, then 5, then 6. Compare the labels and the bars. Try 0 and then -1. Look at both the result and the error area.
after: At 4, A costs 8 and B costs 9. At 5 they tie at 10. At 6, B costs 11 and A costs 12. Zero uses gives 0 for A and 5 for B. A negative count gives an error and no fresh winner.
why: At first a starting fee matters more. With more uses, the per-use part can take over. The tie is a useful test in the middle.
rescue: If both bars look full at 4, give them a shared maximum. Check the printed numbers even when the picture looks right.

premise: Show which titles were added, removed or changed between two small lists.
before: Old rows: S1=Map, S2=Guide. New rows: S1=Map, S2=Field Guide, S3=Rules.
try: Compare the samples. Check every group against the three IDs. Delete S1 from the new list and compare. Then add a second S2 in the new list and compare again.
after: S1 is the same, S2 is renamed from Guide to Field Guide, S3 is added. None are removed. S1 becomes removed. The repeated S2 gets a clear error before a new comparison is shown.
why: An ID is like a tag tied to the file. Changing the words on the cover need not mean it is a new file.
rescue: If S2 looks removed and added, match IDs before comparing titles. Do not use the title as the matching key.

premise: Run two timed puzzle rounds. A manual clock makes pause, resume and scoring easy to test.
before: Round one lasts 3 ticks. Solve button earns 2 points. Round two also lasts 3 ticks.
try: Start, Tick, Pause, then try Solve. Resume and Solve once. Start the next round and Tick three times. Replay and solve both rounds before time runs out. Try Solve again after the final screen.
after: The paused Solve earns nothing. Round one earns 2. Round two times out at 0. Final score is 2. Replay starts fresh. Two quick solves earn 4. A later click cannot add to 4.
why: A timer, a round number and a score each change for different reasons. Test a paused clock separately from a finished clock.
rescue: If the paused Solve earns points, give both Tick and Solve the same running-state check.

premise: Add rows that happened on the same day, then find the busiest day. A tie needs room on the page too.
try: Load the four data rows. Read each day total and the peak list. Change the last count from 0 to 7. Add another line with the same date and a blank count. Run again.
after: The totals are 5, 5 and 0. January 1 and 2 share the peak. January 3 alone leads with 7. The blank on line 6 is listed for review. It does not replace the stored 7.
why: One day's pile can have several slips. Add each pile first, then compare the totals. Looking at the biggest single slip gives a different question.
rescue: If only one date shows in the original tie, collect all days whose total matches the high score.

premise: A search can find the right box even if text carries extra spaces. Check what happens when two rows share a label.
before: Test boxes: Q1 Support active, Q2 Support paused, Q3 Stores active.
try: Search for SUP with extra spaces. Select Q2. Turn on Active only and look at the detail area. Clear the search while keeping Active only checked. Search stone. Turn the filter off and clear the search.
after: First Q1 and Q2 appear. Active only leaves Q1 and clears the old Q2 details. The active list shows Q1 and Q3. Stone has no matches. The last clear shows all three rows.
why: A row's displayed name can repeat. Its ID tells the detail panel exactly which row the reader chose.
rescue: If Q2 details linger after filtering, test whether its ID is still visible before drawing the detail panel.

premise: Let readers edit a round and see the new total. Cancel should take them back to the saved version.
before: Saved rounds: R1=4 and R2=7. Start total is 11. Use -2 for the R2 edit.
try: Edit R2 to -2. Compare both totals before saving. Cancel once. Repeat the edit and Save. Clear R1, try Save, then enter 0 and save. Restore the sample.
after: Before saving the draft is 2 and the saved total is 11. Cancel restores 11. Saving the second edit changes the saved total to 2. A blank blocks the save. With R1 zero and R2 -2 the saved total becomes -2. Reset brings back 11.
why: A draft is like pencil on scratch paper. It should change the official score only when the reader chooses Save.
rescue: If typing immediately changes the saved total, keep separate copies of the draft and saved rows until Save succeeds.

premise: Run a four-question quiz from the first turn through the final score. Give each team exactly two chances.
before: Keys in order: sun, moon, red, blue. Ask four matching questions, each with a correct and a wrong button. Team order is Gold, Green, Gold, Green.
try: Get questions one and four right and the other two wrong. Try pressing an answer after it has been locked. Replay. Answer questions one and three right and the others wrong. Try advancing past the fourth question.
after: Gold and Green each score 1. The final screen says Tie. Another answer on a locked question earns nothing. Gold wins 2 to 0. The page stays on the result until Replay. The new game started with both teams at zero.
why: A game is fair when the team on screen, the team awarded the point and the saved turn order all agree.
rescue: If Gold gets credit for Green's answer, record the answer and score before moving to the next team's turn.

premise: Read a fake mailbox list, mark rows reviewed, then save and restore the handoff. A classmate should be able to check the whole trip.
before: Rows: M1 Queue=4, M2 Queue=0, M3 Queue empty. Checked status starts false for each.
try: Mark M1 and M2 reviewed. Export the file, restore the sample, then import the export. Check each row and both totals. Try a file with version 99, then one with M1 listed twice. Reopen the HTML while the network is off, load the good export again and run its checks.
after: The restored handoff says 2 of 3 reviewed and 4 known items. M2 keeps 0, M3 says Missing. The review flags survive the trip. Both bad files give errors and leave the current handoff untouched. Offline, the good export still restores the same three rows and both totals.
why: The file carries the work between sessions. Checking the whole file before replacing the screen keeps a bad import from spoiling a good handoff.
rescue: If a failed import wipes the list, read the new file into a temporary list. Replace the old list only after every row passes.

premise: Give a player a secret number and a useful hint after each guess.
before: Secret 7. Guesses 3, 9, 7.
try: Open the browser game. Enter 3 and then 9. Read the two clues before entering 7. Write a tally mark each time a real guess goes in. Try a blank during a fresh round, then make one valid guess.
after: 3 gives Higher, 9 gives Lower and 7 gives Found in 3 guesses. The blank shows a hint and leaves the turn count at zero. The valid guess uses turn one.
why: A known secret makes the first round easy to check. Random play can come after that.
rescue: If an empty box uses a turn, check the text before turning it into a number.

premise: A card should hide its answer until the player turns it over.
before: Pier → Dock; Port → Harbor; Stern → Back.
try: Flip the first card and say its answer out loud. Click Next and check whether the new card gives its answer away too soon. Flip the third card. Tap Start over and look for the first answer.
after: Pier shows first. Show answer reveals Dock. Next shows Port and hides Harbor. The deck returns to Pier with Dock hidden. The reader can play again.
why: A card has two facts: which card this is and which side faces up.
rescue: If Harbor shows as soon as you move, reset the face-up flag when the card number changes.

premise: Turn two small counts into a clear bar with a labeled amount.
before: Used 6 blocks; limit 8 blocks.
try: Divide six blocks into a group of eight slots. On paper that leaves two empty slots. Compare your drawing with the bar. Set Used to 0 with Limit 8. Then set Limit to 0.
after: Six of eight fills three quarters of the bar. The label reads 75%. The first case reads 0%. The second asks for a limit and displays no percentage.
why: A percentage tells how much of the whole is used. With no whole to divide by, the number has no meaning.
rescue: If zero usage gives an error, check the limit separately from the used count.

premise: Pack three items and leave the page. See what the page remembers.
before: Badge, Hat, Water. Check Hat only.
try: Check Hat and read the count. Reload using the same address. The box next to Hat should still contain a check. Check Water, reload, then press Clear all.
after: After tapping Hat, the page reads 1 of 3. On reload Hat stays checked. The saved count first reads 2 of 3. Clear all returns to 0 of 3.
why: Packing is a set of yes-or-no choices. Saving one value per item lets you unpack just one item.
rescue: If every box changes together, give each item its own key and label.

premise: Let a reader choose which path to take through a short story.
before: Start has Pier and Hill. Pier ends at a boat. Hill ends at a bell.
try: Write Start on two lines. Add Pier to the first line and Hill to the second. Run the game twice to compare its trails with yours. Pick Hill after the restart. Look at the new path and ending.
after: Choosing Pier shows the boat and Start → Pier. Restart shows both paths. The end shows a bell and Start → Hill. Pier is absent from this run.
why: The page remembers each choice for one trip. Starting over needs a fresh trail.
rescue: If an old choice remains, clear the path list when Restart is pressed.

premise: Build buttons that filter a little list by mail state.
before: Q1 queued; Q2 sent; Q3 queued.
try: Put Q1 and Q3 on a slip marked queued. Put Q2 on a slip marked sent. Each button should show exactly one of your piles. Switch back to All, then repeat Queued twice.
after: Queued lists Q1 and Q3, count 2. Sent lists Q2, count 1. All lists all three. Two taps on Queued still list only Q1 and Q3 once each.
why: A filter changes which rows you see. It keeps the original rows ready for the next filter.
rescue: If each tap adds a second copy, clear the view before drawing the matches.

premise: Use a two-by-two board to learn which moves are legal.
before: Top row 1,2. Bottom row empty,3. Goal 1,2 / 3,empty.
