try: Place four squares on paper with one left open. Try the two moves with a coin on each filled square before trying them on screen. Press Reset. Tap 1, then tap 1 again to put it back.
after: Tapping 2 diagonally does nothing. Tapping 3 moves it left and wins in one move. The original board is back. The count is 2 and the game has not declared a win.
why: Two cells touch only if they share a side. Check row and column before swapping them.
rescue: If a diagonal works, look for a rule that compares only the cell numbers.

premise: A chart should show missing readings differently from zero minutes.
before: A=0 min; B=8 min; C=blank; D=4 min.
try: Sketch bars for 8 and 4 on graph paper. Give A the number 0 and C a question mark. Compare all four labels with the tool. Set B to 0. Refresh the chart and inspect D and C.
after: B has the longest bar. D is half as long. A reads 0. C reads missing. D now sets the full scale at 4. C is still missing.
why: A blank says nobody measured. A zero says someone measured and found no wait.
rescue: If C turns into zero, keep blank text separate before converting numbers.

premise: Find the free gaps in a short practice calendar.
try: Draw the full hour as a strip and color both busy blocks. Measure the gaps at the left and right ends before changing the limit. Increase the minimum to 15 and add a booking from 09:45 to 09:50.
after: At minimum 10 the gaps are 09:00–09:10 and 09:40–10:00. Neither end gap reaches 15. Show No free slot.
why: Draw each booking as shaded squares on a strip. Free runs can occur at either end of the strip.
rescue: If an empty gap appears at 09:25, check that two blocks which touch become one busy period.

premise: Share a total in whole cents so the pieces add back up.
before: Ten cents to split among three seats in seat order.
try: Deal ten coins to three seats in order. Each seat gets three, and the extra coin returns to seat one. Check the displayed sum. Try zero cents and three seats. Then try ten cents and zero seats.
after: The first seat gets 4 cents. The other seats get 3 each. The sum is 10. The first test gives three zero shares. The second asks for at least one seat.
why: Three equal rounded shares can lose a cent. Hand the remaining cents out one at a time.
rescue: If the shares are all 3, compare their sum with the starting ten cents.

premise: Compare yesterday’s practice list with today’s. Report who joined and who left.
before: Yesterday: box-a, box-b. Today: BOX-B, box-c, box-c.
try: Write yesterday on the left and today on the right. Match the two versions of box-b. Compare the items left over on each side. Copy today’s list into both boxes and compare again.
after: Added box-c, removed box-a, kept box-b. Each occurs once. Added and Removed are empty. Kept contains box-b and box-c.
why: Crossing out matches on two lists leaves only the new and missing items.
rescue: If BOX-B looks new, use a cleaned copy for matching before listing the results.

premise: A six-card board can be checked because you know every pair.
before: Fixed deck: sun, moon, star, sun, moon, star. Number slots 1–6.
try: Number the deck positions. A mismatch uses the first try, then the three known pairs use three more. Keep a paper tally beside the board. Match 2 with 5 and 3 with 6. Then press Restart.
after: Tap 1 then 2. The mismatch counts as one try. Continue hides both. Tap 1 then 4: sun stays up. The win message says 4 tries. Restart hides all six and sets tries to 0.
why: A turn begins on the first card and ends on the second. A card cannot be its own pair.
rescue: If you can tap a third card before Continue, pause the board while a mismatch is showing.

premise: Catch bad rows before an app adds anything to a saved list.
before: Saved ID K0. New rows K1,3 and K2,-1. Rule: counts are whole numbers of zero or more.
try: Look at the preview before pressing Apply. Point to the exact bad data row. Open the saved list to check that its old member is still there. Change K2 to 0 and apply once. Try to apply the same rows again.
after: The negative count flags row 2 of the data. The saved list still contains only K0. The first apply adds K1 and K2. The next preview flags those saved IDs and leaves three total.
why: Seeing a preview is like checking a shopping basket before paying. It should not change the saved list.
rescue: If K1 appears after the failed test, collect all errors before writing any new row.

premise: Build a whole playable word game, then close the network and finish the round.
before: Fixed board rows CAT, ORE, DOG. Targets CAT, DOG, COD. Straight paths forward or backward.
try: Trace CAT across the first row, DOG across the last row and COD down the first column. Keep one target for the offline part of the test. Find DOG, go offline after the app says ready, reload, then select COD from top to bottom. Restart.
after: Tap the ends of CAT and then the ends of CAT in reverse. Only one target is checked. COD is in column one. The win message shows all 3. Restart clears the checks and leaves the same playable board while offline.
why: Use a fixed board to prove every clue exists. Save the app files and the player’s progress separately.
rescue: If the page fails offline, check that you first served it at localhost or HTTPS and loaded every file online.

premise: Make a small offline dashboard that can explain every total to a reader.
before: Box A shared 4; B user 0; C room 3; D shared blank. Group by type. Only user and shared boxes belong.
try: Make separate notes for included boxes, known item sum and missing counts. B increases the first total by one and the second by zero. Save the good summary. Add a second A with count 9 and try to import. Then fix D to 2 in a clean copy and import it.
after: The included count is 3. Known items sum to 4. One count is missing and one room is excluded. The user filter shows B with 0. The duplicate is rejected and the good summary stays. Fixing D gives 6 known items and no missing count.
why: A report can have a real zero and still have missing data on another row. Separate those cases before adding anything.
rescue: If the duplicate silently wins, ask for a whole-file ID check before the preview can become the current report.

premise: Turn three rows into a score table that updates whenever a player adds points.
before: Paste Team and Points as headings. Data: Blue 3, Gold 4, Blue -1.
try: After entering the three rounds, add only Blue’s rows by hand. Change one cell inside the table and see whether the total moves by the same amount. Add Gold,0 and Blue,5 within the table. Check both totals.
after: Blue totals 2 points. Gold totals 4. Reading the rows by hand gives the same numbers. Gold stays at 4. Blue rises to 7. Both new rounds are visible.
why: A sum-by-team formula only adds numbers on rows carrying the team’s label.
rescue: If Blue stays at 2, check that the added row is inside the Excel table or formula range.

premise: Have Copilot host a game one question at a time, using answers that you can prove.
before: Deck: How many sides on a square? 4. Which is colder, ice or steam? ice. What is 3 plus 5? 8.
try: Keep three answer slips face down. Reply once per turn, then cross out each slip after the host grades it. Check the final points yourself. Reply steam, then 8. Start a fresh round after seeing the result.
after: Answer 4 first. The score is 1 and only the second question is shown. The final score is 2 of 3. A fresh round starts at 0 and asks about the square.
why: A host must know the answer but keep it out of the question. Check its score after every turn.
rescue: If it reveals the deck, start a new chat with the host directions and tell it to wait after each question.

premise: Three pretend boxes need short, consistent labels you can copy into a guide.
before: A: shared, Help Desk. B: user, Practice Seat. C: room, Meeting Room.
try: Hold the source row and the output label side by side. Read the type inside brackets, then the name outside them. Change only C to test the format. Change C’s name to Training Room. Regenerate the labels and compare them line by line.
after: A reads [shared] Help Desk. B reads [user] Practice Seat. Only C’s label changes. It now reads [room] Training Room.
why: Putting the type in the label helps someone pick the right item without guessing from its name.
rescue: If all labels become capital letters, ask it to keep the original short names exactly as supplied.

premise: Show how much time remains as a meeting moves through its agenda.
before: Start with 30 minutes. Welcome 5, demo 12, questions 8.
try: Start at 30 and cross off 5, 12 and 8 minutes in order. Check each running value before trying the longer final item. Change questions from 8 to 15 minutes. Check the last row again.
after: After the three items the times left are 25, 13 and 5. The last row now shows -2 and Over. Earlier rows still show 25 and 13.
why: Subtract each activity from the time still in the pot. A negative amount tells you how far past the end you went.
rescue: If every row starts from 30, point the formula at the row just above it before subtracting.

premise: Let the player sort made-up messages into a folder based on two short rules.
before: Rules: [help] goes to Help; [bill] goes to Bills; any other tag goes to Review. Cards: [help] printer, [bill] paper, [other] hello.
try: Write the three folder names at the top of a sheet. Place the subject cards below their tags. Compare the host’s grading with your piles. Reply Review to hello. Ask to play again.
after: Reply Help to the printer card. One point. Reply Help to the paper card. The score stays 1 and the explanation points to [bill]. The round ends at 2 of 3. The next game shows the first card and a zero score.
why: Rules that look only at tags are easy to test. A word in the subject should not change the tag rule.
rescue: If the host says hello belongs in Help, ask it to name the card’s tag and apply the third rule.

premise: Build a sheet that tells you when a session fills up.
before: Capacity 3. Input rows: Desk A yes, Desk B no, Desk C yes.
try: Draw three empty seats. Place a token for each yes and none for no. The fourth yes goes beside the seats to show the extra booking. Change Desk B to yes, then try adding Desk D yes.
after: Two seats are taken and one is open. A no does not use a seat. Three yes rows show Full. A fourth flags Over by 1 rather than advertising a negative open seat.
why: The capacity is a fixed number. Every yes uses one place, even if four places were promised by mistake.
rescue: If no uses a seat, check that the counting formula looks for the word yes, not every filled cell.

premise: Create a small Excel tool that tells you which items need a look today.
before: Sample today is day 12. Items opened on days 7, 10, 12 and 13. Watch starts at age 3.
try: Subtract the opened day from day 12. For a result below zero, check the date. Only then apply Watch to ages of three or more. Change today from 12 to 13. Keep the four opened days in place.
after: The four rows read 5 Watch, 2 Fresh, 0 Fresh and Check date. The rows now read 6 Watch, 3 Watch, 1 Fresh and 0 Fresh.
why: One clock cell changes all ages at once. A future start date is worth checking before you trust it.
rescue: If only the first row works, keep the reference to the today cell fixed when filling the formula down.

premise: Make a helper that asks one question at a time and can admit when it has run out of rules.
before: Rule card: cannot find a message → ask “Is search working?” If yes, check folder; if no, check search status. Cannot send → check Outbox. Anything else → human review.
try: Trace the cannot-find path with a pencil. At the question, follow the no branch and stop at its action. Try another path in a fresh turn. Start over with cannot send. Start over again with “picture is crooked.”
after: Say cannot find a message, then no. The helper recommends checking search status and shows that path. The send case points to Outbox. The picture case ends in human review.
why: A little decision tree can guide the next step without guessing the cause of a problem.
rescue: If the helper adds steps about passwords, ask it to read back only the supplied paths and retry.

premise: Play a small number game with a fixed draw order that includes a repeat.
before: Board 2, 4, 6. Draw pile 4, 4, 2, 6. Start with nothing marked.
try: Write 2, 4 and 6 on paper. Cross out each only once when the host calls it. Record draws on a separate line to see the repeat. Draw twice more. Ask for New game, then draw once.
after: After the first two Draws only 4 is marked. The second 4 is labeled a repeat. The fourth draw wins with 2, 4, 6. The reset game has just 4 marked after its first draw.
why: The pile counts every draw. The board counts each number only once. Those are different totals.
rescue: If the repeat earns another square, have the caller keep an explicit set of the board numbers it already marked.

premise: Make an Excel view that catches real overlaps while allowing back-to-back bookings.
before: Room A: slot 1 starts at minute 10 and ends at 25. Slot 2 runs 25–40. Slot 3 runs 20–27.
try: Draw three strips for the time slots. Two strips touch and two pairs share actual time. Then put the third strip on a separate row for room B. Move slot 3 to room B and recalculate the pair list.
after: Slots 1 and 2 can touch with no clash. Pairs 1/3 and 2/3 clash. There are no room conflicts after the move. The times did not change.
why: A room matters as much as the clock. A booking that ends when another starts frees the room in time.
rescue: If 1/2 is flagged, check whether a less-than sign changed to less-than-or-equal.

premise: A team needs to know who can read a file and who can edit it. Group names alone do not answer that.
before: Desk A belongs to Readers and Editors. Desk B belongs to Readers. Readers can view Kit. Editors can edit Kit. Edit includes view.
try: Put a pencil mark beside each group Desk A belongs to. Follow each group to its rights on Kit and circle the strongest right you find. Remove A from Editors. Add Desk C without a group. Rebuild the chart.
after: Desk A can edit through Editors. Desk B can view through Readers. A and B can view Kit. C has None. No desk can edit after the change.
why: A membership list tells you which groups to ask. A grant tells you what each group can actually do.
rescue: If C gets view, ask for the row that connects C to Readers. There should be none.

premise: Try to keep a tiny project within its budget. Each choice changes the remaining amount.
before: Start with 10 tokens. Round 1 map 3 or clue 1. Round 2 bridge 5 or raft 2. Round 3 lantern 4 or torch 1.
try: Keep a running balance after each accepted choice. At 2 tokens you cannot buy the 4-token lantern. Check whether the host offers a new choice. Try lantern. After it is declined, choose torch instead.
after: Choose map, then bridge. The balance runs 10, 7, 2. The finished list is map, bridge, torch. One token remains. The declined lantern cost nothing.
why: A bad choice should leave a player exactly where they were, able to choose again.
rescue: If a rejected purchase advances the round, require both a valid choice and enough tokens before moving on.

premise: One item should have only one borrower at a time. Let people trace the result to a line.
before: Events: 1 take A desk1; 2 take A desk2; 3 return A desk1; 4 take A desk2.
try: Write Available beside item A. Erase and replace its holder only when a row is accepted. Row 2 should leave the name written by row 1. Add row 5 return A desk1, then row 6 return A desk2.
after: The decisions are accepted, rejected, accepted, accepted. Desk2 holds A at the end. Row 5 is rejected and preserves desk2. Row 6 makes A available.
why: The state after one line is the starting state for the next. A rejected line leaves that state alone.
rescue: If row 2 takes A, have the worksheet look at the holder after row 1 before applying the next event.

premise: Build a playable two-team race. Keep the score sheet ready for the next game.
before: Target 8. Rounds: Blue 5, Gold 3, Blue -2, Gold 5. Zero is a legal turn. Blank means no turn.
try: Play each score in order. Circle the first row whose team total reaches the target. Changing the target changes which row you circle. Change the target to 5. Then start a new game ID, enter Blue 0 and a blank score.
after: At target 8, Gold wins on round 4. Blue has 3 and Gold has 8. At 5, Blue first wins on round 1. The new game counts one round and keeps both totals at zero. The prior game’s rows remain.
why: Separating setup, input and the board lets you check the math without losing the game record.
rescue: If clearing a new game wipes old rows, filter by game ID. Keep each game’s inputs in the same history table.

premise: A support group wants one workbook that can explain its summary and catch bad input.
before: Sample columns ID,Type,Count. A,shared,2; B,user,0; C,room,4; D,user,blank. Count only user and shared rows.
try: Add 2 and 0. Write D on a separate missing list. Check that the room’s 4 stays out of the included sum before fixing the missing count. Give D a count of 5. Check the heading. Add a second A and check the heading again.
after: Three rows belong. Known sum is 2. D is missing, C is excluded and the heading says Hold. The clean result is Ready and the known sum is 7. The repeat changes the heading to Hold and points to A.
why: A reader needs the reason a report is held as well as the totals. Keep checks linked to row IDs so a person can find the source.
rescue: If a missing count passes because its cell looks like zero, check whether the original input cell is blank before doing math.

premise: Your first tiny app needs a button, a number and a way to start over.
before: Start 0. Count button adds 2. Reset returns to 0.
try: Make a paper trail of counts: 0, 2, 4, 0. Tap the app in the same sequence. Test one button press using the keyboard too. Use the Tab key to move to Count by two. Press Enter once, then press Reset.
after: Two taps give 2 and then 4. Reset gives 0. The keyboard press gives 2 just like a tap. Reset returns to 0.
why: Starting small makes it easy to spot the first thing that went wrong. Both ways of pressing a button should do the same job.
rescue: If Enter adds four, check whether both the click handler and a second key handler ran for the same press.

premise: Search by item code and show a useful message for a code the list never had.
before: T1 hat; T2 blue bag; T3 mug.
try: Read the full label beside T2 in the source before searching. Remove the spaces and lower the capitals in your head, then compare the match. Search T9, then Clear, then T1.
after: Entering “ t2 ” shows blue bag. T alone shows Unknown tag. T9 shows Unknown tag. Clear empties the field and old result. T1 shows hat.
why: When the code identifies one item, matching only the first letter can point to the wrong item.
rescue: If T returns all three, ask for exact code matching after spaces and capitals are cleaned.

premise: Sometimes a report needs to spot an empty or unclear subject in a pile of practice notes.
before: Subjects: Trip; two spaces; Plan update. Minimum length 5 after trimming.
try: Count the four letters in Trip on your fingers. For two spaces, trim both ends and count again. Plan update includes its middle space. Enter “ Plans ” including the outside spaces.
after: Trip gives 4 and Too short. Two spaces gives 0 and Missing. Plan update gives 11 and Ready. The reported length is 5 and the word is Ready.
why: Trim first so a stray space cannot make a four-letter subject pass.
rescue: If a blank is called short, check for zero length before checking the under-five rule.

premise: A player checks three things they think belong in a kit. Make the answers easy to verify.
before: Choices: map, key, bell. Correct set: map and bell.
try: Place one token beside each correct pick and take one away for key. Count the remaining tokens before looking at the app’s score. Try again, then select map and bell only and press Check.
after: Picking only map earns 1. Picking all three earns 1 because key costs one point. The result is 2 of 2 with no wrong picks. Reset unchecks all three.
why: A score alone cannot teach the player much. Show the missed choices after they commit to an answer.
rescue: If the score changes on every extra tap of Check, calculate it from the selected boxes each time.

premise: A small counter helps a writer stay inside a limit.
before: Limit 12. Sample “Meet at pier” has 12 characters including spaces.
try: Count each space in Meet at pier. Save that exact note, then compare the writing field with the saved note after adding the exclamation point. Add an exclamation point. Try saving. Then erase the draft.
after: Typing Meet at pier shows 0 left and allows Save. The saved area shows the phrase. The extra character shows 1 over. Save is off. The previous saved note stays visible in both cases.
why: What you are typing and what you last saved are two different things. One can change without changing the other.
rescue: If an over-limit edit changes the saved area, update that area only when Save succeeds.

premise: Draw every card from a small deck once. Shuffle only when a new round begins.
before: Fixed test deck bell, key, rope, flag.
try: Write down each card as it leaves the pile. If all four cards have left, there is no card for a fifth draw. Check the pile before and after reset. Try Draw again, then New deck. Draw once in the reset test deck.
after: Four draws give bell, key, rope and flag in test mode. The remaining counts are 3, 2, 1, 0. The extra draw cannot create a fifth card. The reset deck starts with bell and 3 remaining.
why: Pulling a card out of the pile prevents it appearing twice before the pile is rebuilt.
rescue: If a card repeats early, inspect the remaining deck after each draw. Make sure the picked card has left it.

premise: Build a whole turn game, including the rules after someone wins.
before: Start at 0 for both. Blue rolls 4, Gold 3, Blue 6. Target 10.
try: Write the teams down in turn order. Add 4 to Blue, 3 to Gold, then 6 to Blue. Draw a line under the winning turn. Press Roll again after the win, then Restart. Inspect the first team and both scores.
after: Blue reaches 10 on turn three. Gold remains at 3. The winner says Blue. The extra press has no effect. Restart puts Blue first with 0 to 0.
why: A game has a state for playing and one for finished. Recording that state keeps later taps from changing a win.
rescue: If Gold gets a fourth turn, check for a winner before handing over the turn.

premise: Undo should reverse the last choice, including two orders of the same thing.
before: Juice 2 tokens, toast 3, fruit 1. Order juice, toast, juice.
try: Write each purchase on its own slip. For Undo, remove the last slip only. Add the remaining prices yourself before you trust the display. Undo twice more. Try Undo on empty, then add fruit.
after: The first three choices total 7. Undo removes only the last juice and leaves 5. The order reaches zero without going below it. Fruit starts a fresh order totaling 1.
why: A list of moves lets you step backward one move at a time. A total by itself forgets what was ordered last.
rescue: If both juices disappear, remove the last list entry instead of all entries with its name.

premise: A service can return an empty middle page while later pages still have results.
before: Page 1 items A,B next 2. Page 2 empty next 3. Page 3 item C next none.
try: Follow the number after next. Draw an arrow from the empty middle page to page 3. On the second run, check where an arrow returns to a page already read. Make page 3 point back to 2. Run again and count the visits.
after: The clean run visits pages 1, 2, 3 and returns A, B, C in order. The reader flags a loop after exactly three different pages. It does not return the partial list as complete.
why: An empty page can still point forward, like a blank page in the middle of a book. Only the next-page mark tells you where to go.
rescue: If C goes missing, see whether an empty items list mistakenly ends the loop.

premise: A player changes one letter per move to reach the final word.
before: Start CAT, goal DOG. Allowed: CAT, COT, COG, DOG. Try CAT → COT → COG → DOG.
try: Compare the letters one at a time in CAT and COT. Try the same check with DOG. Only after counting changes do you check the allowed list. Start over. Try CAT to DOG directly and CAT to MAT, then type “ cot ”.
after: The three moves reach DOG and win in 3. COT is a valid first move. The first move changes too many letters. MAT is outside the list. The third works and counts as move 1.
why: Rules must all pass before the app adds a move. A word can look close and still fail the allowed-list check.
rescue: If a bad move changes the count, show the error first and return before adding to the history.

premise: A task may depend on another task finishing first. Make that order clear.
before: Read input has no earlier task. Make report needs Read input. Review needs Make report.
try: Write the three tasks as a chain. Cross out the first check. Trace both links to find which later checks lose their support. Finish all three, then uncheck Read input. Inspect the later tasks and their reasons.
after: Checking Read input unlocks Make report. Checking Make report unlocks Review. Both later tasks become unchecked and locked. The finish count returns to 0 of 3.
why: A tower cannot keep its top blocks in place after its base is removed. A check can depend on earlier checks.
rescue: If Review stays done, follow the chain past the first task that became invalid.

premise: Two equal-sized files can be different. Test what your tool treats as a match.
before: A.txt has blue. B.txt has blue. C.txt has gold. All three words have four letters.
try: Count the bytes in blue and gold. Their lengths agree. Then read each letter side by side to see why matching size alone gives a wrong group. Change B.txt to gold and add a new empty D.txt. Run the finder again.
after: A.txt and B.txt share a group. C.txt stands alone even though all sizes match. B and C now group together. A and D stand alone. The tool leaves every file in place.
why: Two boxes can weigh the same and contain different things. Compare the contents before declaring a match.
rescue: If C joined the first group, ask for a final check of file bytes rather than just the length.

premise: A table must explain a tie without picking a winner by accident.
before: Blue 7, Gold 7, Green 4. Put equal scores at the same rank; next rank skips the tied slot.
try: Write down the number of teams strictly above each team, then add one for its rank. Two teams with nobody above them both get rank one. Change Green to 8, reload, and compare all ranks. Then reset.
after: The ranks are Blue 1, Gold 1, Green 3. Both top teams are marked joint leaders. Green is 1. Blue and Gold share rank 2. After reset the original scores and tie return.
why: Alphabetical order makes the screen steady. It should never break a real points tie.
rescue: If Gold is called second at 7, compare its points with the previous team before assigning a new rank.

premise: Finish and test a local game with turns, hidden tiles, a score and a clear end.
before: Fixed 2×3 grid slots 1–6 contain coin, blank, coin, gem, blank, coin. Coin=1, gem=3. Turns alternate Blue then Gold.
try: Follow the six legal picks on paper. Leave the repeated pick off your turn list. Give the gem three points and each coin one. Continue with 2, 3, 5 and 6. Read the winner and replay. Test all buttons with the keyboard.
after: Pick 1, then 4, then 1 again. Blue has 1 and Gold 3. The repeat leaves Blue’s turn in place. The final scores are Blue 1 and Gold 5. Replay covers all six tiles and returns the first turn to Blue.
why: A fixed board lets two people check the same scores. Hiding a used tile again during a round would make the proof fall apart.
rescue: If the winner differs, write down who owned each legal pick and check whether the repeated 1 wrongly used a turn.

premise: Combine a before-and-after report, a download and a test that protects a good result.
before: Before A=user, B=shared, C=user. After A=user, B=user, D=shared. IDs are pretend and match without case.
try: Match the two A rows and the two B rows before checking for additions or removals. Read the type on each side of B to spot the change. Save the good report. Add a second b to After and compare. Then restore the original input and download again.
after: The clean run shows D added, C removed, B changed from shared to user and A the same. Every ID appears once. The duplicate case shows a row error and keeps the last good result. The restored download matches all four expected entries.
why: Two snapshots tell you which rows changed. A bad snapshot can make an entire group seem to vanish, so check both lists first.
rescue: If B and b become separate boxes, check each ID after cleaning spaces and case but before building the comparison.

premise: Practice reading a result before scoring a tool. This made-up example could come from any builder.
before: The first game opens at Blue 0, Gold 0. Blue gets Question 1 right. The first tap shows Blue 2, Gold 0.
try: Tap the same choice again straight away. Look at both totals, the question number and the active team. Finish the game and check the other four rules on the page.
after: Suppose the second tap changes Blue to 4. Mark the click-lock check Fail and record both scores. If all four other checks pass, the first-try score is 4 out of 5.
why: Two taps on one answer count as just one pick. The number on the screen lets another reader repeat your check.
rescue: If the screen changes too fast to tell, restart and repeat the double tap. Leave the check untested until you can tell what happened. Keep this first file when you try the later edit.
